author: Seneca
text: Life is not short; we waste much of it. We guard our money carefully but hand out our hours to anyone who asks. Treat time as your scarcest asset.
q: According to Seneca, why does life feel short?
a: Because we waste it, guarding money but giving time away freely.
action: Before saying yes to any request today, ask: is this worth an hour of my life?

author: Seneca
text: Rehearse misfortune in advance. Spend a few minutes imagining loss or hardship, and you will find it less frightening and appreciate what you have more.
q: What is the purpose of 'premeditating adversity'?
a: To reduce fear of misfortune and increase gratitude for the present.
action: Spend 2 minutes imagining losing something you take for granted, then appreciate it.

author: Seneca
text: We suffer more in imagination than in reality. Most of what we fear never happens, and what does happen is rarely as bad as the dread before it.
q: What does Seneca say we suffer more from?
a: Imagination — anticipated troubles rather than real ones.
action: Write down one worry and label it: happening now, or only imagined?

author: Seneca
text: Read deeply in a few great authors rather than skimming many. Scattered reading is like constant travel: you meet many hosts but make no friends.
q: Why does Seneca warn against reading too widely?
a: Scattered reading leaves nothing rooted; depth in a few authors builds real understanding.
action: Pick one book and reread a chapter instead of starting something new.

author: Seneca
text: Each day, take one idea from your reading and digest it. A single thought lived with all day does more than a hundred skimmed.
q: What practice does Seneca recommend after each day's reading?
a: Select one idea to digest and carry through the day.
action: Choose one sentence from today's session and repeat it to yourself at lunch.

author: Seneca
text: Practise poverty occasionally: live a few days on plain food and rough clothing. You will discover that what you feared losing is easily endured.
q: What does Seneca suggest to lose the fear of poverty?
a: Periodically live simply on purpose and see that it's bearable.
action: Have a deliberately simple, cheap meal today and notice that you are fine.

author: Seneca
text: Anger is a brief madness. The best cure is delay: let the first wave pass before you speak or act, because almost nothing done in anger is done well.
q: What is Seneca's best remedy for anger?
a: Delay — wait before acting on it.
action: When irritated today, wait ten breaths before responding.

author: Seneca
text: Associate with people who will make you better, and welcome those you can make better. Character is contagious in both directions.
q: Whom does Seneca advise us to spend time with?
a: Those who improve us and those we can improve.
action: Message someone who brings out your best and set up a meeting.

author: Seneca
text: Fortune gives and takes. Hold wealth, status and comfort as things on loan, ready to return them without bitterness.
q: How should we hold external goods, per Seneca?
a: As loans from fortune, ready to give them back.
action: Look at a possession you value and say: 'This is on loan.'

author: Seneca
text: 'Luck is what happens when preparation meets opportunity.' Do the quiet work now so you can seize chances when they appear.
q: What turns opportunity into luck?
action: Spend 15 minutes preparing for an opportunity you hope will come.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Each morning, expect to meet difficult people: the ungrateful, the arrogant, the dishonest. Expecting them removes the shock, and remembering they act from ignorance removes the anger.
q: What does Marcus prepare himself for each morning?
a: Meeting difficult people — so he is neither shocked nor angered.
action: This morning, predict one difficult interaction and decide your calm response.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'You have power over your mind — not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.' Your judgments, not events, disturb you.
q: According to Marcus, what actually disturbs us?
a: Our judgments about events, not the events themselves.
action: When upset today, ask: what story am I telling myself about this?

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'The impediment to action advances action. What stands in the way becomes the way.' Every obstacle is material to practise a virtue on.
q: What did Marcus say about obstacles?
a: The obstacle becomes the way — a chance to practise virtue.
action: Name today's biggest obstacle and the virtue it lets you practise.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do every act as if it were the last of your life: without carelessness, pretence or complaint. This gives ordinary tasks dignity and focus.
q: How does Marcus advise performing each action?
a: As if it were your last — fully, without pretence or complaint.
action: Do one routine task today with full attention, as if it mattered most.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Picture the view from above: cities, empires, and lifetimes as tiny and brief. Your problems shrink to their true size.
q: What is 'the view from above'?
a: Imagining the vast scale of the world to put problems in perspective.
action: Close your eyes for a minute and zoom out from your room to the planet.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'Waste no more time arguing what a good man should be. Be one.' Theory without practice is decoration.
q: What does Marcus tell himself instead of debating virtue?
a: Stop arguing about what a good person is — be one.
action: Replace one opinion you'd share today with one good action.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The best revenge is not to be like the one who wronged you. Answer rudeness with steadiness, not imitation.
q: What is the best revenge, according to Marcus?
a: Not becoming like the person who wronged you.
action: If someone is rude today, deliberately respond with courtesy.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Everything is change. Fame, bodies and grievances are all flowing away like a river. Clinging to anything fixed is the root of distress.
q: Why should we not cling to things, says Marcus?
a: Everything is constantly changing and passing away.
action: Notice one thing you're clinging to and loosen your grip on it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When you want to cheer yourself up, think of the good qualities of the people around you: one's energy, another's modesty, another's generosity.
q: What does Marcus recommend for lifting your mood?
a: Reflect on the virtues of people around you.
action: List three people and one virtue each. Tell one of them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Get up in the morning to do the work of a human being. You were not made to lie warm under the covers but to act and contribute.
q: What argument does Marcus use against staying in bed?
a: We were made to do human work, not for comfort.
action: Get up at the first alarm tomorrow — decide it tonight.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it is not right, do not do it; if it is not true, do not say it. Two simple rules cover most moral confusion.
q: What are Marcus's two quick rules?
a: If not right, don't do it; if not true, don't say it.
action: Catch and drop one small exaggeration in conversation today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Retreat into yourself. No place is quieter than your own mind, available any moment for renewal.
q: Where does Marcus say the best retreat is?
action: Take a 3-minute mental retreat: eyes closed, slow breaths.

author: Epictetus
text: Some things are up to us — our opinions, choices and efforts — and some are not: body, reputation, outcomes. Peace comes from focusing only on the first.
q: What is the dichotomy of control?
a: Distinguishing what's up to us (judgments, choices) from what isn't (outcomes, others).
action: Sort today's worries into two columns: in my control / not.

author: Epictetus
text: People are disturbed not by things, but by their opinions about things. Change the opinion and the disturbance dissolves.
q: What disturbs people according to Epictetus?
a: Their opinions about things, not things themselves.
action: Reframe one frustration today in neutral words.

author: Epictetus
text: If you want to improve, be content to appear foolish. Progress requires asking basic questions and being a beginner in public.
q: What must you accept to make progress, says Epictetus?
action: Ask one 'stupid' question you've been avoiding.

author: Epictetus
text: Wish things to happen as they actually happen, and your life will flow well. Fighting reality only adds a second wound.
q: What does Epictetus advise wishing for?
a: That things happen as they actually do.
action: When plans change today, say 'Good, this is what's happening' and adapt.

author: Epictetus
text: When you lose something, say 'I have returned it' rather than 'I have lost it.' Everything is borrowed.
q: How should we speak of losses, according to Epictetus?
a: 'I have returned it' — treating everything as borrowed.
action: Reframe one recent loss as something returned.

author: Epictetus
text: We have two ears and one mouth so we can listen twice as much as we speak.
q: What does Epictetus infer from our ears and mouth?
a: Listen twice as much as you speak.
action: In your next conversation, ask questions and let others talk first.

author: Epictetus
text: Don't explain your philosophy — embody it. At a banquet, don't lecture on how to eat; eat as one should.
q: What does Epictetus say to do instead of explaining principles?
action: Act on one principle today without mentioning it to anyone.

author: Epictetus
text: No one is free who is not master of himself. Freedom is not having what you want but not being ruled by wants.
q: How does Epictetus define freedom?
a: Self-mastery — not being enslaved to desires.
action: Skip one small craving today on purpose.

author: Epictetus
text: Any person capable of angering you becomes your master. Guard your reactions so others don't hold your controls.
q: What happens when someone can easily anger you?
action: Notice who 'pushes your buttons' and decide not to hand them control.

author: Viktor Frankl
text: Between stimulus and response there is a space. In that space lies our freedom to choose our response, and in our response lies our growth.
q: What lies between stimulus and response?
a: A space containing our freedom to choose.
action: Pause one full breath before reacting to anything today.

author: Viktor Frankl
text: Those with a 'why' to live can bear almost any 'how'. Meaning is the strongest source of resilience.
q: What allows people to endure almost any hardship?
a: Having a 'why' — a meaning or purpose.
action: Write one sentence: what is my 'why' this year?

author: Viktor Frankl
text: Meaning is found in three ways: by creating work or doing deeds, by experiencing something or loving someone, and by the attitude we take to unavoidable suffering.
q: What are Frankl's three sources of meaning?
a: Work/deeds, love/experience, and attitude toward suffering.
action: Do one thing today in each category, however small.

author: Viktor Frankl
text: Don't aim at success or happiness directly. They ensue as side effects of dedication to a cause greater than yourself.
q: How, per Frankl, do happiness and success come?
a: As side effects of devotion to something beyond ourselves.
action: Spend 20 minutes on something for someone else, not for yourself.

author: Viktor Frankl
text: Everything can be taken from a person but one thing: the last of human freedoms — to choose one's attitude in any given circumstances.
q: What is the 'last of human freedoms'?
a: Choosing one's attitude in any circumstances.
action: In a frustrating moment today, consciously choose your attitude.

author: Viktor Frankl
text: Live as if you were living for the second time and had acted as wrongly the first time as you are about to act now.
q: What is Frankl's 'second time' imperative?
a: Live as if you're living a second time and already made the mistake you're about to make.
action: Before one decision today, imagine you've already regretted the wrong choice.

author: Viktor Frankl
text: It is not what we expect from life, but what life expects from us. Life asks questions; we answer through responsible action.
q: How does Frankl reverse the question of meaning?
a: Ask what life expects from us, not what we expect from life.
action: Ask: what is life asking of me today? Do that thing.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Be proactive: focus on your circle of influence, not your circle of concern. Working on what you can affect makes that circle grow.
q: What's the difference between the circles of concern and influence?
a: Concern is all we care about; influence is what we can affect. Proactive people focus on influence.
action: Pick one concern and identify the one action within your influence.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Begin with the end in mind. Imagine your own funeral: what would you want people to say? Let that shape today's choices.
q: What exercise does Covey use for 'begin with the end in mind'?
a: Imagining your funeral and what you'd want said about you.
action: Write three words you'd want said about you, and act on one.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Put first things first. Important-but-not-urgent work (planning, health, relationships) is where effectiveness lives, yet it's always crowded out by urgency.
q: Which quadrant does Covey say matters most?
action: Block 30 minutes today for one important, non-urgent task.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Seek first to understand, then to be understood. Most people listen with the intent to reply; listen to grasp the other's view.
q: What is Covey's habit 5?
a: Seek first to understand, then to be understood.
action: In one conversation, summarise the other person's view before giving yours.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Think win-win. Treat life as cooperative, not a zero-sum contest. Look for solutions where both sides benefit, or make no deal.
q: What is the alternative Covey proposes if win-win isn't possible?
action: In a negotiation or disagreement today, state what the other side needs too.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Make deposits in the emotional bank account: keep promises, show kindness, apologise sincerely. Trust is built in small deposits.
q: What builds the 'emotional bank account'?
a: Small acts: kept promises, kindness, sincere apologies.
action: Make one deliberate deposit with someone close today.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Sharpen the saw: regularly renew body, mind, heart and spirit. A woodcutter too busy to sharpen his saw works harder and achieves less.
q: What are the four dimensions of renewal?
action: Do one small renewal act in each dimension today.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Synergise: the whole is greater than the sum of its parts. Value differences as sources of better ideas rather than threats.
q: What does Covey mean by synergy?
a: Valuing differences to create solutions better than either party alone.
action: Ask someone who thinks differently for their view on your problem.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Ivan Ilyich lived a proper, comfortable, approved life and realised only at death it had been empty. A 'correct' life is not necessarily a true one.
q: What did Ivan Ilyich realise at the end?
a: His proper, conventional life had been empty of real meaning.
action: Ask: which of my habits do I keep only because it looks right?

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: 'All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.' Happiness rests on many basics done right; any single failure can undo it.
q: What does the 'Anna Karenina principle' suggest?
a: Success requires many factors done right; failure needs only one gone wrong.
action: Check one neglected basic in your relationships or health.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: The most important time is now; the most important person is the one you are with; the most important task is to do them good.
q: What are the answers to Tolstoy's three questions?
a: Now; the person in front of you; doing them good.
action: Give the next person you speak with your complete attention.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: 'The two most powerful warriors are patience and time.' Many battles are won by waiting rather than charging.
q: Which two 'warriors' does Kutuzov praise?
action: Identify one situation where waiting is the better move, and wait.

author: Leo Tolstoy
book: How Much Land Does a Man Need?
text: Pahom kept wanting more land until his greed killed him; in the end he needed only six feet. Endless wanting destroys contentment.
q: What is the lesson of 'How Much Land Does a Man Need?'
a: Greed for more is endless and destructive; we need far less than we think.
action: Name one thing you already have 'enough' of and stop seeking more.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Tolstoy found that wealth and fame did not answer 'why live?'. Simple people living by faith and work seemed to have the answer he lacked.
q: What did Tolstoy observe about simple working people?
a: They had a sense of meaning his wealth and fame couldn't provide.
action: Do some simple, physical, useful work today.

author: Leo Tolstoy
text: Everyone thinks of changing the world, but no one thinks of changing himself. Real reform starts at home.
q: What does Tolstoy say most people neglect?
a: Changing themselves rather than the world.
action: Pick one thing you criticise in others and fix it in yourself.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Know the enemy and know yourself, and you need not fear a hundred battles. Self-knowledge is half of every strategy.
q: What does Sun Tzu say ensures victory in a hundred battles?
a: Knowing both the enemy and yourself.
action: Write down your top strength and top weakness for a current challenge.

author: Sun Tzu
text: The supreme art of war is to subdue the enemy without fighting. The best victories avoid conflict entirely.
q: What is the 'supreme art of war'?
action: Resolve one tension today through a conversation instead of a confrontation.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Victorious warriors win first and then go to war; defeated warriors go to war first and then seek to win. Preparation decides outcomes.
q: How do victorious warriors differ from defeated ones?
a: They secure victory through preparation before engaging.
action: Prepare thoroughly for tomorrow's most important meeting or task.

author: Sun Tzu
text: In the midst of chaos there is also opportunity. Disorder in your surroundings can be turned to your advantage if you stay calm.
q: What does Sun Tzu see in chaos?
action: When something goes wrong today, look for the opening it creates.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Be like water: it shapes itself to the ground. Adapt your approach to circumstances rather than forcing a fixed plan.
q: Why does Sun Tzu compare strategy to water?
a: Water adapts to terrain; strategy must adapt to circumstances.
action: Change approach on one stuck problem instead of pushing harder.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Choose your battles. There are roads not to follow, armies not to attack, and positions not to contest.
q: What does Sun Tzu say about which battles to fight?
a: Not every battle is worth fighting; choose carefully.
action: Drop one argument or fight that isn't worth it.

author: Aristotle
text: We become what we repeatedly do. Virtues are built by practice, like a craft: we become brave by doing brave acts.
q: How are virtues acquired, according to Aristotle?
a: Through habit — repeatedly performing virtuous acts.
action: Choose one virtue and do one small act of it today.

author: Aristotle
text: Virtue is a mean between two extremes: courage lies between cowardice and recklessness, generosity between stinginess and waste.
q: What is Aristotle's 'golden mean'?
a: Virtue as the midpoint between excess and deficiency.
action: Identify one trait where you lean to an extreme and nudge toward the middle.

author: Aristotle
text: The highest good is eudaimonia — flourishing — a life of activity in accordance with virtue, over a complete lifetime, not momentary pleasure.
q: What is eudaimonia?
a: Flourishing: virtuous activity across a whole life.
action: Ask: what would a flourishing version of today look like?

author: Aristotle
text: There are three kinds of friendship: of utility, of pleasure, and of virtue. Only the last, based on mutual admiration of character, endures.
q: Which kind of friendship endures, per Aristotle?
a: Friendship of virtue — based on character.
action: Reach out to a friend you admire for who they are.

author: Aristotle
text: Anyone can become angry. But to be angry with the right person, to the right degree, at the right time, for the right purpose — that is hard.
q: What makes anger virtuous, per Aristotle?
a: Right person, right degree, right time, right purpose.
action: If annoyed today, check all four 'rights' before expressing it.

author: Aristotle
text: Persuasion rests on three pillars: ethos (character), pathos (emotion) and logos (reason). Use all three.
q: What are Aristotle's three modes of persuasion?
action: In your next request, include credibility, feeling and a reason.

author: Aristotle
text: 'It is the mark of an educated mind to be able to entertain a thought without accepting it.' Curiosity before judgement.
q: What marks an educated mind?
a: Entertaining an idea without accepting it.
action: Steelman a view you disagree with for two minutes.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Franklin tracked 13 virtues, focusing on one per week and marking lapses daily. Small, systematic self-improvement compounds.
q: How did Franklin work on his virtues?
a: Focusing on one of 13 virtues weekly and tracking daily lapses.
action: Pick one virtue for this week and track it tonight.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Franklin began each day asking 'What good shall I do this day?' and ended asking 'What good have I done today?'
q: What were Franklin's morning and evening questions?
a: 'What good shall I do this day?' / 'What good have I done today?'
action: Ask the morning question now; ask the evening one before bed.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: The Ben Franklin effect: asking someone for a small favour makes them like you more, because people justify helping by liking.
q: What is the Ben Franklin effect?
a: People who do you a favour come to like you more.
action: Ask someone for a small favour or recommendation today.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: 'Early to bed and early to rise makes a man healthy, wealthy, and wise.' Rhythm and rest underpin all achievement.
q: What does Franklin link to early rising?
action: Set a bedtime alarm tonight, 30 minutes earlier than usual.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: 'Lost time is never found again.' Treat minutes as money and you'll spend them better.
q: What did Franklin say about lost time?
action: Track where your time goes for one afternoon.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Franklin stopped contradicting people bluntly and began with 'I imagine' or 'it appears to me'. Modest phrasing won him far more agreement.
q: What phrasing change did Franklin make in arguments?
a: He replaced dogmatic assertions with modest ones like 'it appears to me'.
action: Replace 'You're wrong' with 'I see it differently because…' today.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: 'An investment in knowledge pays the best interest.' Learning compounds over a lifetime.
q: According to Franklin, what investment pays best?
action: Spend 15 minutes learning a skill that will pay off for years.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Don't criticise, condemn or complain. Criticism makes people defensive and rarely changes behaviour.
q: What is Carnegie's first principle?
action: Go a full day without complaining. Restart the count if you slip.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Become genuinely interested in other people. You make more friends in two months by being interested in them than in two years trying to get them interested in you.
q: How does Carnegie say you make friends fastest?
a: By being genuinely interested in others.
action: Ask someone three follow-up questions about their life.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: A person's name is to them the sweetest sound in any language. Remember and use it.
q: What did Carnegie say about names?
a: A name is the sweetest sound to its owner — remember and use it.
action: Use the name of everyone you speak with today.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: The only way to win an argument is to avoid it. Even if you win, the other person resents you.
q: How do you get the best of an argument, per Carnegie?
action: Let one argument go today, even if you're right.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: If you are wrong, admit it quickly and emphatically. It disarms the other person and earns respect.
q: What should you do when you're wrong, per Carnegie?
action: Own one recent mistake openly.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Talk in terms of the other person's interests. To influence someone, show how something gets them what they want.
q: How do you influence people, per Carnegie?
a: Talk in terms of their interests and wants.
action: Frame one request today around what the other person gains.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living
text: Live in 'day-tight compartments'. Shut out yesterday's regrets and tomorrow's fears; deal only with today.
q: What are 'day-tight compartments'?
a: Living only in today, closing off past and future.
action: When worry about tomorrow arises, say 'Not today's job.'

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Stop Worrying and Start Living
text: Ask: what is the worst that could happen? Accept it mentally, then calmly work to improve on it.
q: What is Carnegie's three-step worry formula?
a: Ask the worst case, accept it, then work to improve on it.
action: Apply the formula to one worry in writing.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Do nothing which is of no use. Strip away wasted motion in combat and in life.
q: What is one of Musashi's simplest rules?
a: Do nothing which is of no use.
action: Eliminate one useless task or habit from today.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Perceive what cannot be seen with the eye. Train both broad 'perception' and narrow 'sight' to read situations deeply.
q: What two kinds of seeing does Musashi distinguish?
action: In one meeting, notice the mood and what's unspoken.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Mastery is reached through daily practice over years: 'a thousand days of training to forge, ten thousand days to polish'.
q: What does Musashi say mastery requires?
a: Long, daily practice — thousands of days.
action: Do 10 minutes of deliberate practice on your core skill.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Do not regret what you have done. Learn the lesson, then put the act behind you.
q: What does Musashi say about regret?
a: Do not regret your past actions.
action: Write a lesson from a regret, then let the regret go.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Know the ways of all professions. Understanding other crafts sharpens your own.
q: Why should one study other crafts, per Musashi?
a: Understanding other ways deepens mastery of your own.
action: Learn how someone in a different field solves a problem.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Do not pursue pleasure for its own sake. Pleasure pursued becomes a master.
q: What is Musashi's view on pleasure-seeking?
a: Don't pursue pleasure for its own sake.
action: Postpone one pleasure today and notice your freedom.

author: Lao Tzu
text: 'A journey of a thousand miles begins with a single step.' Begin small; the beginning matters more than the plan.
q: Where does a long journey begin?
action: Take the smallest first step on a project you've been delaying.

author: Lao Tzu
text: Water is soft yet wears away stone. Gentleness and persistence overcome hardness and force.
q: What does water teach in the Tao Te Ching?
action: Approach one conflict today softly instead of forcefully.

author: Lao Tzu
text: He who knows others is wise; he who knows himself is enlightened. Mastering others is strength; mastering yourself is true power.
q: What does Lao Tzu call true power?
action: Spend five minutes journaling about why you reacted as you did recently.

author: Lao Tzu
text: When you are content to be simply yourself and don't compare or compete, everyone will respect you.
q: What does Lao Tzu say brings respect?
a: Being content as yourself without comparing or competing.
action: Notice one comparison you make today and drop it.

author: Confucius
text: When you see a worthy person, think of becoming equal to them. When you see an unworthy one, examine yourself inwardly.
q: What should we do on meeting unworthy people, per Confucius?
a: Examine ourselves for the same faults.
action: When someone annoys you today, check whether you share that flaw.

author: Confucius
text: 'It does not matter how slowly you go as long as you do not stop.' Consistency beats speed.
q: What matters more than speed, per Confucius?
action: Do your habit today even if only for two minutes.

author: Confucius
text: Do not impose on others what you would not wish for yourself. The silver rule as foundation of all ethics.
q: What is Confucius's version of the golden rule?
a: Don't do to others what you wouldn't want done to you.
action: Before one decision affecting others, picture yourself in their place.

author: Confucius
text: Learning without thinking is useless; thinking without learning is dangerous. Combine study and reflection.
q: What's wrong with learning without thought?
a: It's useless; and thought without learning is dangerous.
action: After this session, reflect for 2 minutes on one card.

author: Plato
text: 'The unexamined life is not worth living,' said Socrates. Regular self-examination is what makes life human.
q: What did Socrates say about the unexamined life?
action: Spend five minutes tonight reviewing your day honestly.

author: Plato
text: In the allegory of the cave, prisoners mistake shadows for reality. Education is turning the soul toward the light, which is uncomfortable at first.
q: What does the cave allegory represent?
a: Mistaking appearances for reality; education as turning toward truth.
action: Question one belief you hold only because everyone around you does.

author: Plato
text: Socrates was wise because he knew that he did not know. Intellectual humility opens the door to learning.
q: Why did the oracle call Socrates wise?
a: He knew that he knew nothing.
action: Say 'I don't know' honestly at least once today.

author: Plato
text: The soul is like a charioteer driving two horses — one noble, one unruly. Reason must guide both spirit and appetite.
q: What does the charioteer represent?
action: Notice when appetite wants control today and let reason take the reins.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: 'Our life is frittered away by detail. Simplify, simplify.' Fewer possessions and commitments leave room to live deliberately.
q: What did Thoreau urge in response to detail?
action: Remove or give away one thing you don't need.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: Thoreau went to the woods to live deliberately and front only the essential facts of life. Deliberate living means choosing, not drifting.
q: Why did Thoreau go to the woods?
a: To live deliberately and confront life's essentials.
action: Spend 20 minutes outdoors without your phone.

author: Henry David Thoreau
text: The cost of a thing is the amount of life you exchange for it. Price everything in hours of your life.
q: How does Thoreau define cost?
a: The amount of life exchanged for it.
action: Convert your next purchase into hours of work before buying.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Trust yourself. Imitation is suicide; envy is ignorance. Your own perspective is worth expressing.
q: What does Emerson call imitation?
action: Share one original idea you've kept to yourself.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: 'A foolish consistency is the hobgoblin of little minds.' Don't cling to past positions just to look consistent.
q: What is the hobgoblin of little minds?
action: Change your mind openly about something when the evidence warrants.

author: Ralph Waldo Emerson
text: Every gain has a cost, and every loss brings something. The universe balances accounts over time.
q: What is Emerson's law of compensation?
a: Every gain has a cost and every loss a compensation.
action: Find the hidden benefit in a recent setback.

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: 'My life has been full of terrible misfortunes, most of which never happened.' Fear invents more than fate does.
q: What did Montaigne say about his misfortunes?
action: Write down one fear and its realistic likelihood.

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: To philosophise is to learn how to die. Familiarity with mortality removes its terror and sharpens life.
q: Why does Montaigne say to philosophise is to learn to die?
a: Contemplating death removes fear and makes life vivid.
action: Reflect for one minute: what would I do if this were my last year?

author: Michel de Montaigne
text: Montaigne asked 'What do I know?' and wrote essays as experiments on himself. Self-study is a lifelong, honest inquiry.
q: What question was Montaigne's motto?
action: Write a short paragraph about a habit of yours, as if studying a stranger.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: All humanity's problems stem from our inability to sit quietly in a room alone. We flee boredom into distraction.
q: What did Pascal identify as the root of human trouble?
a: Inability to sit quietly alone in a room.
action: Sit alone, without input, for five minutes.

author: Blaise Pascal
text: 'I have made this letter longer than usual because I lacked the time to make it shorter.' Brevity takes effort.
q: What did Pascal apologise for in his letter?
a: Its length — he lacked time to make it shorter.
action: Edit your next message to half its length.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Never compete with someone who has nothing to lose. They can risk everything; you can't.
q: Whom does Gracián advise never to compete with?
a: Someone who has nothing to lose.
action: Identify a fight where the other side risks little — and step back.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Know how to say no. A gracious refusal is better than a grudging yes, and it protects your time.
q: What does Gracián say about refusing?
a: A gracious no beats a grudging yes.
action: Decline one request politely today.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Leave others a little hungry. Don't exhaust your welcome or over-satisfy; scarcity preserves value.
q: Why should you leave people 'a little hungry'?
action: End one conversation while it's still good.

author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: Fortune governs half our actions; the other half is left to us. Build dikes in calm weather so the flood can't sweep you away.
q: What does Machiavelli advise doing in calm times?
action: Add to an emergency fund or backup plan today.

author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: Men judge by appearance more than by touch, since everyone can see but few can feel. Manage impressions, but substance must back them.
q: How do people mainly judge, per Machiavelli?
a: By appearances — few experience the substance.
action: Make sure one piece of work today both looks and is excellent.

author: Epicurus
text: Pleasure is the absence of pain in the body and trouble in the soul — not luxury. Simple bread and water give real contentment.
q: How does Epicurus define pleasure?
a: Absence of bodily pain and mental disturbance.
action: Enjoy one very simple pleasure fully today.

author: Epicurus
text: Of all the things wisdom provides for a happy life, the greatest is friendship.
q: What did Epicurus call wisdom's greatest gift for happiness?
action: Share a meal or call with a friend this week — schedule it now.

author: Epicurus
text: Do not spoil what you have by desiring what you have not. What you now own was once among the things you hoped for.
q: What spoils what we have, per Epicurus?
action: Name three things you once wished for that you now have.

author: Buddha
text: We are what we think. With our thoughts we make the world. Guard your mind as you would your home.
q: What does the Dhammapada say we are?
action: Notice one recurring negative thought and replace it.

author: Buddha
text: Holding onto anger is like grasping a hot coal to throw at someone; you are the one who gets burned.
q: What is anger compared to?
a: Grasping a hot coal — you get burned first.
action: Release one grudge in writing.

author: Thomas à Kempis
text: First keep peace within yourself; then you can bring peace to others.
q: What must come before bringing peace to others?
action: Start the day with five quiet minutes before any screen.

author: Boethius
text: Fortune is a turning wheel. Those at the top will fall, those at the bottom will rise. Happiness built on fortune is unstable.
q: What image does Boethius use for fortune?
action: Remind yourself that today's situation, good or bad, will turn.

author: Boethius
text: Nothing is miserable unless you think it so; and every lot is happy to one who bears it calmly.
q: What makes a situation miserable, per Boethius?
action: Describe your current hardest situation in calm, neutral words.

author: Samuel Smiles
text: Great results come from patient, persistent effort by ordinary people, not from genius. Character is built in daily drudgery.
q: What did Smiles see behind great achievements?
action: Do the boring but important task first today.

author: Arthur Schopenhauer
text: What a person is matters more than what he has or how he's regarded. Health and inner riches outweigh wealth and status.
q: Which of Schopenhauer's three categories matters most?
a: What a person is (character, health, mind).
action: Invest an hour in health or mind instead of possessions.

author: William James
text: Make habits your ally: launch new habits with strong initiative, never allow an exception until the habit is rooted, and act on resolutions immediately.
q: What is James's rule about exceptions to new habits?
a: Never allow an exception until the habit is firmly rooted.
action: Pick one habit and promise no exceptions for 7 days.

author: William James
text: Act the way you want to feel. Behaviour changes emotion as much as emotion changes behaviour.
q: What does James say about action and feeling?
a: Acting as if changes how you feel.
action: Stand tall and smile for one minute before a hard task.

author: Napoleon Hill
text: Definiteness of purpose is the starting point of achievement. Write a specific goal and read it daily.
q: What does Hill call the starting point of all achievement?
action: Write one specific goal with a deadline and read it aloud.

author: Samuel Johnson
text: People need to be reminded more often than they need to be instructed. Repetition of known truths is how wisdom sticks.
q: What do people need more than instruction, per Johnson?
action: Review three old cards you already know.

author: Cicero
text: Gratitude is not only the greatest of virtues, but the parent of all the others.
q: What does Cicero call the parent of all virtues?
action: Write a thank-you note or message to someone today.

author: Cicero
text: Each stage of life has its own fitting qualities. Old age need not be mourned if a life has been well spent in learning and service.
q: What makes old age good, per Cicero?
a: A life well spent; each age has its own virtues.
action: Ask an older person what they enjoy about their current age.

author: Ecclesiastes
text: For everything there is a season. Timing matters: a time to plant and a time to reap, a time to speak and a time to be silent.
q: What is the central idea of 'a time for everything'?
a: Each action has its proper season.
action: Ask: is this a season to push or to wait? Act accordingly.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Above all, don't lie to yourself. One who lies to himself loses the ability to see truth in himself or others.
q: What does Zosima warn against above all?
action: Admit one uncomfortable truth to yourself in writing.

author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
text: Active love is harder than love in dreams. Loving humanity in general is easy; loving the person in front of you takes work.
q: What does Dostoevsky contrast with 'love in dreams'?
a: Active love — concrete, effortful care for real people.
action: Do one practical kindness for someone nearby.

author: Victor Hugo
text: Bishop Myriel answered theft with mercy, and it transformed Jean Valjean's life. One act of grace can change a person's trajectory.
q: What turned Jean Valjean's life around?
a: The bishop's mercy after Valjean stole from him.
action: Give someone the benefit of the doubt today.

author: Charles Darwin
text: Darwin kept a note of every fact contradicting his theories, because he knew the mind forgets inconvenient evidence quickly.
q: What did Darwin write down immediately?
action: Note one piece of evidence against a belief you hold.

author: Seneca
text: 'While we are postponing, life speeds by.' Begin at once to live, and count each day as a separate life.
q: What did Seneca say happens while we postpone?
action: Do today one thing you've been 'saving for later'.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'The happiness of your life depends on the quality of your thoughts.' Tend your mind like a garden.
q: On what does happiness depend, per Marcus?
action: Write three thoughts you want to cultivate today.

author: Epictetus
text: First say to yourself what you would be; then do what you have to do. Identity precedes action.
q: What does Epictetus say to decide first?
a: Who you want to be — then act accordingly.
action: Write 'I am someone who…' and do one act that proves it.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Appear weak when you are strong and strong when you are weak. Don't reveal your full hand.
q: What does Sun Tzu say about appearances?
a: Conceal your true strength or weakness.
action: Hold back one card in your next negotiation.

author: Aristotle
text: Man is by nature a social animal. Isolation diminishes us; community is part of a good life.
q: What did Aristotle call humans by nature?
action: Join or contribute to a group activity this week.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Give honest, sincere appreciation. People crave appreciation more than almost anything, and flattery is a counterfeit of it.
q: How does Carnegie distinguish appreciation from flattery?
a: Appreciation is sincere; flattery is insincere.
action: Give one specific, sincere compliment today.

author: Jim Collins
text: Great companies are led by "Level 5" leaders who pair personal humility with fierce resolve for the company. They credit others for success and blame themselves for failure.
q: What two traits define a Level 5 leader?
a: Personal humility and intense professional will.
action: When a job goes well this week, credit the crew by name; when it goes badly, own it first.

author: Jim Collins
text: First get the right people on the bus, then decide where to drive it. The right people make strategy easier; the wrong people make any strategy fail.
q: What comes before deciding direction, per Collins?
a: Getting the right people on the bus (and wrong ones off).
action: Rate each person on your team: would you hire them again today? Note one action.

author: Jim Collins
text: Confront the brutal facts while never losing faith that you will prevail. Optimism that ignores reality breaks people; realism without hope breaks morale.
q: What is the Stockdale Paradox?
a: Face the brutal facts while keeping faith you will prevail.
action: Write down the one ugly number in your business you've been avoiding.

author: Jim Collins
text: The Hedgehog Concept sits where three circles overlap: what you can be best at, what drives your economics, and what you're deeply passionate about.
q: What are the three circles of the Hedgehog Concept?
a: Best in the world at, economic engine, passion.
action: List the job types where you're best AND most profitable. Do more of those.

author: Jim Collins
text: Breakthroughs come from the flywheel: many consistent pushes in one direction that build momentum. There is no single defining moment.
q: What does the flywheel image represent?
a: Momentum built by consistent effort in one direction, not a single big moment.
action: Identify the one repeatable action that grows your business and do it today.

author: Jim Collins
text: Good is the enemy of great. Settling for 'good enough' removes the pressure to become excellent.
q: Why is good the enemy of great?
a: Being 'good enough' removes the drive to become great.
action: Pick one routine part of your work and raise its standard a notch.

author: Jim Collins
text: Great companies keep a 'stop doing' list as carefully as a to-do list. Discipline means saying no to opportunities outside your core.
q: What list did good-to-great companies keep?
action: Write a stop-doing list with three items and drop one this week.

author: Jim Collins
text: Visionary companies preserve a core ideology while stimulating progress in everything else. Values stay; methods change.
q: What do visionary companies keep fixed and what do they change?
a: Fixed core values; everything else evolves.
action: Write the two values your company would never compromise on.

author: Jim Collins
text: Big Hairy Audacious Goals unify people around a bold, clear target with a finish line. They stretch a company more than vague missions do.
q: What is a BHAG?
a: A bold, clear, long-term goal that unifies effort.
action: Set a 10-year goal for your business in one sentence.

author: Jim Collins
text: Fire bullets, then cannonballs: test ideas cheaply before betting big. Calibrate with small shots, then commit fully to what works.
q: What does 'bullets then cannonballs' mean?
a: Test small and cheap first; commit big resources only after evidence.
action: Test a new service with one small job before investing in new equipment.

author: Jim Collins
text: The 20-mile march: hit steady targets in good times and bad. Consistency beats bursts of heroic effort followed by collapse.
q: What is the 20-mile march?
a: Steady, consistent progress regardless of conditions.
action: Set a minimum weekly target you will hit whatever the weather.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: Most small businesses are started by technicians who love the work, not entrepreneurs who build systems. Doing the work is different from running a business.
q: What is the 'entrepreneurial myth'?
a: That knowing the technical work means you know how to run a business doing it.
action: Block one hour this week to work ON the business, not in it.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: Every business owner wears three hats: entrepreneur, manager and technician. Healthy businesses balance all three.
q: What are Gerber's three personalities?
action: Note which hat you wore most this week and which you neglected.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: Build your business as if it were a franchise prototype to be copied 5,000 times. That forces you to systematise everything.
q: Why imagine your business as a franchise prototype?
action: Write a one-page checklist for your most common job type.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: Systems run the business; people run the systems. Good systems let ordinary people produce extraordinary results.
q: What runs the business, per Gerber?
action: Document how a site should look when the crew leaves for the day.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: Create an organisation chart with positions, even if you fill them all. It reveals which jobs exist and which you must eventually hand off.
q: Why draw an org chart when you're alone?
a: To see every role and plan which to delegate.
action: Draw your org chart with roles, and put your name where you currently fill them.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: Your business is not your life. It should serve your life goals, not consume them.
q: What should the business serve?
action: Write what you want your business to give your life in 5 years.

author: Eric Ries
text: Build, measure, learn. Make the smallest version that tests your idea, measure real behaviour, and learn before scaling.
q: What is the core loop of the Lean Startup?
action: Test one new offer on three customers before printing anything.

author: Eric Ries
text: A minimum viable product is the simplest thing that teaches you whether customers want it. Perfection before feedback is waste.
q: What is an MVP for?
a: Learning what customers really want with minimum effort.
action: Offer a new service verbally to customers before building a price list.

author: Eric Ries
text: Pivot or persevere: at regular intervals, decide on evidence whether to change course or keep going. Don't drift.
q: What decision should be made regularly?
action: Review one service that isn't working: pivot it, drop it, or push on.

author: Eric Ries
text: Beware vanity metrics like total enquiries; track actionable ones like conversion and repeat rate.
q: What's the difference between vanity and actionable metrics?
a: Vanity metrics look good; actionable ones guide decisions.
action: Calculate what share of your quotes became jobs last month.

author: Peter Thiel
text: Competition is for losers: the best businesses create a niche they dominate rather than fighting rivals on price.
q: Why does Thiel dislike competition?
a: It drives profits to zero; monopoly niches earn more.
action: Name one niche where you could be the obvious local choice.

author: Peter Thiel
text: Ask: what important truth do very few people agree with you on? Secrets are the source of new value.
q: What is Thiel's contrarian question?
a: What important truth do few people agree with you on?
action: Write one thing you know about your industry that others miss.

author: Peter Thiel
text: Start small and dominate a small market, then expand. Too big a market at first means you own none of it.
q: Where should a new business start?
action: Pick one neighbourhood or customer type to dominate this season.

author: Peter Thiel
text: Distribution matters as much as product. A great service nobody hears about fails.
q: What do engineers often underestimate, per Thiel?
action: Spend 30 minutes on marketing today, not on operations.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: Reciprocity: people feel obliged to return favours. Giving first, genuinely, opens doors.
q: What is the reciprocity principle?
a: People feel compelled to return what they receive.
action: Give a client a free small extra (like site tidying) and don't mention it.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: Commitment and consistency: once people take a small public step, they tend to stay consistent with it.
q: How does commitment influence behaviour?
a: People act consistently with prior commitments.
action: Ask clients to agree a small step (site visit) before the big quote.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: Social proof: when unsure, people follow what similar others do. Show that people like them chose you.
q: What is social proof?
a: People follow others' behaviour when uncertain.
action: Ask two happy customers for a review or a photo of their finished job.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: Authority: people defer to credible experts. Signal expertise honestly through credentials, uniforms and clear knowledge.
q: How can you ethically use authority?
a: Show genuine expertise and credentials clearly.
action: Add your certifications and years of experience to your quote template.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: Liking: we say yes to people we like — those similar to us, who compliment us, and cooperate with us.
q: What factors increase liking?
action: Find common ground with a client before discussing price.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: Scarcity: things seem more valuable when they are rare or disappearing. Honest limits raise perceived value.
q: Why does scarcity persuade?
a: Rare or limited things seem more valuable.
action: Tell clients honestly how many slots you have left this season.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: What you focus someone's attention on just before a request shapes their answer. The moment before matters.
q: What is pre-suasion?
a: Shaping attention just before a message to influence response.
action: Show a finished-job photo before presenting the quote.

author: Chris Voss
text: Tactical empathy: show you understand the other side's feelings and view. Understanding is not agreement, but it unlocks cooperation.
q: What is tactical empathy?
a: Deliberately understanding and voicing the other's perspective.
action: In your next negotiation, name the other person's concern before your own.

author: Chris Voss
text: Mirroring: repeat the last few words someone said, with an upward tone. It makes them keep talking and reveal more.
q: What is mirroring?
a: Repeating the last few key words to encourage elaboration.
action: Mirror a supplier or client three times in one conversation.

author: Chris Voss
text: Labelling: name the emotion you sense — 'It seems like you're worried about the timeline.' Naming defuses it.
q: How does labelling help in negotiation?
a: Naming emotions defuses negative ones and builds rapport.
action: Use 'It sounds like…' once in a difficult conversation.

author: Chris Voss
text: Aim for 'that's right', not 'you're right'. 'That's right' means they feel truly understood.
q: Which phrase signals a breakthrough?
action: Summarise a client's problem until they say 'that's right'.

author: Chris Voss
text: Ask calibrated 'how' and 'what' questions: 'How am I supposed to do that?' makes the other side solve your problem.
q: What are calibrated questions?
a: Open 'how/what' questions that make the other side think about your constraints.
action: When pushed on price, ask 'How am I supposed to do that for this amount?'

author: Chris Voss
text: 'No' is not failure; it makes people feel safe. Ask no-oriented questions like 'Is it a bad idea to…?'
q: Why seek a 'no'?
a: It makes people feel safe and in control, opening dialogue.
action: Ask a slow-paying customer: 'Have you given up on settling this?'

author: Chris Voss
text: Don't split the difference. Meeting halfway often produces a bad deal for both. Hold your value and find creative terms.
q: Why not split the difference?
a: Compromise often yields poor outcomes; creative terms are better.
action: Offer a different scope instead of a lower price next time.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Know where your time goes. Record it, cut what's useless, and consolidate the rest into large blocks.
q: What is Drucker's first step to effectiveness?
a: Record and analyse where your time goes.
action: Log your time for one full workday.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Effective executives ask 'What can I contribute?' rather than 'What am I owed?' Focus on results outside yourself.
q: What question focuses effort on contribution?
action: Ask what single contribution would most help your customers this month.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Build on strengths — your own and others'. Staff for strengths, not to minimise weaknesses.
q: What does Drucker say to build on?
action: Give each crew member the task they're best at tomorrow.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Do first things first, one thing at a time. Concentration is the secret of effectiveness.
q: What is Drucker's secret of effectiveness?
a: Concentration — one thing at a time.
action: Work 90 minutes on one task with your phone off.

author: Peter Drucker
text: The purpose of a business is to create a customer. Marketing and innovation are the two basic functions.
q: What is the purpose of a business, per Drucker?
action: Ask a recent customer why they chose you.

author: Peter Drucker
text: What gets measured gets managed — but measure the right things. Wrong measures distort behaviour.
q: What's the risk of measuring the wrong things?
action: Choose one number that truly reflects job quality and track it.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Innovation is systematic: look for unexpected successes, failures, and changes in demand. Most opportunities hide in surprises.
q: Where does Drucker say innovation opportunities often hide?
a: In the unexpected — surprises in success, failure and demand.
action: Write down the most unexpected request you got this year. Is it a market?

author: Andrew Grove
text: A manager's output is the output of their team plus the teams they influence. Your job is leverage.
q: How does Grove define a manager's output?
a: The output of their organisation and those they influence.
action: Spend 30 minutes teaching a crew member a skill that multiplies their output.

author: Andrew Grove
text: One-on-ones are high-leverage: a short regular meeting where the report sets the agenda.
q: Who sets the agenda in a Grove one-on-one?
action: Have a 15-minute one-on-one with an employee and let them lead.

author: Andrew Grove
text: Find the limiting step in your production and plan around it. The bottleneck sets the pace.
q: What does Grove say determines production flow?
action: Identify the bottleneck on your current job — machine, truck or permit.

author: Andrew Grove
text: Watch for strategic inflection points — moments when the fundamentals of your industry shift. Spot them early.
q: What is a strategic inflection point?
a: A moment when industry fundamentals change dramatically.
action: List one change (rules, tech, prices) that could reshape your trade.

author: Andrew Grove
text: Task-relevant maturity determines management style: new people need structure; experienced ones need autonomy.
q: What should determine how closely you manage someone?
action: Give one experienced worker more freedom on their next task.

author: Gary Keller
text: Ask: what's the one thing I can do such that by doing it everything else becomes easier or unnecessary?
q: What is the Focusing Question?
a: What's the ONE thing I can do such that everything else becomes easier or unnecessary?
action: Ask the focusing question about your business this morning.

author: Gary Keller
text: Time-block your most important work first thing, and protect it like an appointment.
q: How does Keller protect the ONE thing?
a: Time-blocking it and defending the block.
action: Block the first hour tomorrow for your most important task.

author: Gary Keller
text: Success is sequential, not simultaneous. Like dominoes, small wins topple bigger ones.
q: What does the domino effect illustrate?
a: Success builds sequentially from small to large.
action: Pick today's first domino and knock it down before lunch.

author: Brian Tracy
text: Do your hardest, most important task first thing in the morning. Everything after feels easier.
q: What is 'eating the frog'?
a: Doing the hardest important task first.
action: Make the call you're dreading before 9 a.m.

author: Brian Tracy
text: Apply the 80/20 rule: 20% of your tasks produce 80% of results. Focus there.
q: What does the 80/20 rule say about tasks?
action: Find the 20% of customers who give 80% of profit.

author: Brian Tracy
text: Plan every day in advance, the night before. Ten minutes of planning saves hours.
q: When should the day be planned?
action: Write tomorrow's plan tonight in 10 minutes.

author: James Clear
text: Get 1% better every day; small improvements compound into remarkable results.
q: What compounds over time in Atomic Habits?
action: Improve one tiny thing in your daily routine.

author: James Clear
text: You don't rise to the level of your goals; you fall to the level of your systems.
q: What matters more than goals, per Clear?
action: Turn one goal into a daily system.

author: James Clear
text: Make good habits obvious, attractive, easy and satisfying; invert these for bad habits.
q: What are the four laws of behaviour change?
a: Make it obvious, attractive, easy, satisfying.
action: Make one habit easier by preparing what you need tonight.

author: James Clear
text: Every action is a vote for the type of person you want to become. Identity-based habits last longer than outcome-based ones.
q: What are actions, per Clear's identity view?
a: Votes for the person you want to become.
action: Do one action today that proves 'I run a professional company'.

author: James Clear
text: Habit stacking: attach a new habit to an existing one — 'After I pour coffee, I'll check today's jobs.'
q: What is habit stacking?
a: Linking a new habit to an existing one.
action: Stack one business habit on your morning coffee.

author: James Clear
text: Environment beats motivation. Design your space so the right action is the easy one.
q: What beats motivation, per Clear?
action: Organise the truck so the most-used tools are within reach.

author: James Clear
text: The two-minute rule: scale a new habit down to something that takes two minutes. Show up first, then improve.
q: What is the two-minute rule?
a: Start a habit with a version that takes two minutes.
action: Do two minutes of bookkeeping today.

author: James Clear
text: Never miss twice. Missing once is an accident; missing twice starts a new habit.
q: What's the rule after slipping on a habit?
action: If you skipped a habit yesterday, do it today no matter what.

author: Cal Newport
text: Deep work — focused, distraction-free effort — produces the most value and is increasingly rare.
q: Why is deep work valuable?
a: It produces high value and is rare.
action: Do one 60-minute deep-work block on quoting or planning.

author: Cal Newport
text: Schedule every minute of your workday in blocks. Planning reveals where time leaks.
q: What does Newport recommend doing with your workday?
action: Block tomorrow's day in 30-minute chunks.

author: Cal Newport
text: Shut down work at a fixed time with a ritual. Rest improves the next day's focus.
q: Why use a shutdown ritual?
a: It ends work cleanly so the mind can rest and recharge.
action: End today by reviewing tomorrow's list and saying 'shutdown complete'.

author: Cal Newport
book: So Good They Can't Ignore You
text: Passion follows mastery. Build rare and valuable skills, and passion will grow from competence.
q: What does Newport say comes before passion?
a: Mastery of rare and valuable skills.
action: Pick one skill that would make you rare in your trade and practise it.

author: Greg McKeown
text: Less but better. Pursue fewer things with full energy rather than many half-heartedly.
q: What is the essentialist motto?
action: Cut one low-value activity from your week.

author: Greg McKeown
text: If it's not a clear yes, it's a clear no. Use strict criteria for commitments.
q: What is McKeown's 90% rule?
a: If something isn't a clear yes (90%+), it's a no.
action: Turn down one job that doesn't fit your best work.

author: Greg McKeown
text: Protect the asset — you. Sleep and recovery are prerequisites for high contribution.
q: What is the asset to protect?
action: Sleep 8 hours tonight.

author: Greg McKeown
text: Build buffers: add 50% to time estimates. Things take longer than we expect.
q: How much buffer does McKeown suggest?
action: Add buffer days to your next job schedule.

author: Eliyahu Goldratt
text: The goal of a business is to make money now and in the future. Every activity should be judged by that.
q: What is 'the goal'?
a: To make money now and in the future.
action: Check whether today's tasks contribute to profit.

author: Eliyahu Goldratt
text: An hour lost at a bottleneck is an hour lost for the whole system. An hour saved elsewhere is a mirage.
q: Why is bottleneck time so valuable?
a: Lost bottleneck time is lost system output.
action: Keep your bottleneck machine running during lunch by staggering breaks.

author: Eliyahu Goldratt
text: Theory of Constraints: identify the constraint, exploit it, subordinate everything else, elevate it, repeat.
q: What are the five focusing steps?
action: Apply step one: name your constraint this month.

author: Eliyahu Goldratt
text: Local efficiency can hurt the whole. Keeping everyone busy can create piles of useless work.
q: Why can local efficiency be harmful?
a: It can create excess inventory and hide the real constraint.
action: Stop one task done just to look busy.

author: Gino Wickman
text: Every business has six key components: vision, people, data, issues, process and traction. Strengthen each.
q: What are the six EOS components?
a: Vision, people, data, issues, process, traction.
action: Score your business 1–10 on each of the six.

author: Gino Wickman
text: Rocks: set 3–7 priorities per quarter. Everything else waits.
q: What are 'Rocks'?
action: Write your three Rocks for the next 90 days.

author: Gino Wickman
text: A weekly scorecard of 5–15 numbers tells you the health of the business at a glance.
q: What is a scorecard?
a: A weekly set of key numbers.
action: Make a 5-number weekly scorecard: quotes, jobs won, revenue, cash, hours.

author: Gino Wickman
text: Identify, Discuss, Solve: tackle issues one at a time by root cause, not by talking endlessly.
q: What is the IDS process?
action: Take one recurring problem through IDS today.

author: Gino Wickman
text: Right people, right seats: people must share core values (right person) and have the capacity for their role (right seat).
q: What defines 'right person, right seat'?
a: Shares values, and gets, wants and has capacity for the role.
action: Check one role: is the right person in the right seat?

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Take profit first: Sales − Profit = Expenses. Pay yourself before costs, and the business adapts.
q: What is the Profit First formula?
action: Open a separate profit account and move 1% of today's income there.

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Use separate bank accounts for profit, owner's pay, tax and operating expenses. Physical separation guides behaviour.
q: Why separate accounts?
a: Visible separation prevents spending money meant for profit and tax.
action: Set up a dedicated tax account this week.

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Parkinson's Law applies to money: expenses rise to meet available cash. Less available, more creative.
q: How does Parkinson's Law apply to money?
a: Spending expands to match available money.
action: Review subscriptions and cancel one you don't need.

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Design the business to run without you. Identify the Queen Bee Role — the one thing that makes the business thrive — and protect it.
q: What is the Queen Bee Role?
a: The core function most critical to the business's success.
action: Name your Queen Bee Role and ensure it's covered every day.

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Your time should shift from doing to deciding to delegating to designing.
q: What are the four Ds of time in Clockwork?
action: Move one task from 'doing' to 'delegating' this week.

author: Alex Hormozi
text: Make an offer so good people feel stupid saying no. Value = dream outcome × likelihood ÷ (time delay × effort).
q: What is Hormozi's value equation?
a: Dream outcome × perceived likelihood ÷ (time delay × effort).
action: Rewrite one service offer to reduce the customer's effort.

author: Alex Hormozi
text: Charge more. Higher prices allow better service, better staff and happier customers.
q: Why does Hormozi argue for higher prices?
a: They fund better delivery and attract better clients.
action: Raise prices on your most in-demand service by 5–10%.

author: Alex Hormozi
text: Guarantees reduce perceived risk. A strong, specific guarantee can boost sales more than discounts.
q: What does a guarantee reduce?
action: Draft a clear guarantee, e.g. 'site left clean or we return free'.

author: Alex Hormozi
text: To get leads, do more of the core four: warm outreach, cold outreach, content, and paid ads.
q: What are the 'core four' lead methods?
a: Warm outreach, cold outreach, content, paid ads.
action: Contact five past customers today to ask for referrals.

author: Alex Hormozi
text: Niche down: a specific offer to a specific audience commands higher prices.
q: Why niche down?
a: Specific offers for specific audiences command premium prices.
action: Write a service offer aimed at one specific customer type.

author: Jocko Willink
text: Leaders own everything in their world. No excuses, no blame — only ownership.
q: What is extreme ownership?
a: Taking full responsibility for all outcomes in your world.
action: Own one problem today that you'd normally blame on others.

author: Jocko Willink
text: There are no bad teams, only bad leaders. Standards are set by what the leader tolerates.
q: What does Willink say about bad teams?
a: There are no bad teams, only bad leaders.
action: Address one sloppy standard you have been tolerating.

author: Jocko Willink
text: Prioritise and execute: when overwhelmed, pick the highest-priority problem and attack it.
q: What's the method when facing multiple problems?
a: Prioritise and execute — one at a time.
action: When stressed today, write problems down and solve the top one.

author: Jocko Willink
text: Simple: plans and orders must be simple and clear so everyone understands them.
q: Why must plans be simple?
action: Explain tomorrow's job plan to the crew in three sentences.

author: Jocko Willink
text: Commander's intent: explain the why, so people can make good decisions without you.
q: What is commander's intent?
a: The purpose behind the plan, enabling independent decisions.
action: Tell the crew why a job matters, not just what to do.

author: Jocko Willink
text: Discipline creates freedom: routines and rigour give you control over your time and options.
q: How does discipline create freedom?
action: Get up at the same time tomorrow and start without delay.

author: Ben Horowitz
book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
text: There's no recipe for hard problems. Leaders must make decisions in the 'struggle' without clear answers.
q: What does Horowitz call the difficult period every founder faces?
action: Make one decision you've been postponing.

author: Ben Horowitz
book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
text: Take care of the people, the products and the profits — in that order.
q: In what order should leaders take care of things?
action: Ask a worker what would make their job easier.

author: Ben Horowitz
book: The Hard Thing About Hard Things
text: When delivering bad news to staff, be direct and honest. Sugar-coating erodes trust.
q: How should bad news be delivered?
action: Deliver one overdue piece of feedback clearly and kindly.

author: Jason Fried & DHH
text: Planning is guessing. Make decisions as you go, based on what you know now.
q: What does Rework say about long-term plans?
a: They're guesses; decide as you go.
action: Replace a long plan with next week's three priorities.

author: Jason Fried & DHH
text: Embrace constraints: limited time, money and people force creativity and focus.
q: How are constraints useful?
action: Solve one problem today without spending money.

author: Jason Fried & DHH
text: Say no by default. Every yes costs focus and future flexibility.
q: What's Rework's default answer?
action: Decline one small request that distracts from core work.

author: Jason Fried & DHH
text: Underdo the competition: do less, but better and simpler.
q: How should you compete, per Rework?
a: Do less but better and simpler.
action: Remove one service that complicates your business.

author: Daniel Kahneman
text: System 1 thinks fast and intuitively; System 2 thinks slow and deliberately. Big decisions deserve System 2.
q: What are System 1 and System 2?
a: Fast intuitive thinking and slow deliberate thinking.
action: Sleep on one big purchase before deciding.

author: Daniel Kahneman
text: The planning fallacy: we underestimate time and cost by focusing on the best case. Use past similar jobs as reference.
q: What is the planning fallacy?
a: Underestimating time and cost by assuming the best case.
action: Compare your next estimate to the actual time of three similar past jobs.

author: Daniel Kahneman
text: Loss aversion: losses hurt about twice as much as equal gains feel good. It can make us too cautious.
q: What is loss aversion?
a: Losses feel about twice as painful as gains feel good.
action: Frame a decision as both gain and loss to see it clearly.

author: Daniel Kahneman
text: Anchoring: the first number mentioned strongly influences negotiations. Set the anchor yourself.
q: What is anchoring?
a: The first number heavily influences judgement.
action: Lead with your price in your next negotiation.

author: Daniel Kahneman
text: Run a premortem: imagine the project failed and list why. It surfaces risks optimism hides.
q: What is a premortem?
a: Imagining a project has failed and explaining why, before it starts.
action: Do a 5-minute premortem on your next big job.

author: Clayton Christensen
text: Successful companies fail by listening too well to current customers while cheaper, simpler disruptors grow from below.
q: Why do good companies get disrupted?
a: They serve existing customers while ignoring simpler, cheaper innovations.
action: Watch one low-cost competitor and note what they do well.

author: Clayton Christensen
text: Customers 'hire' products to do a job. Understand the job and you understand demand.
q: What is jobs-to-be-done?
a: Customers hire a product to accomplish a job in their lives.
action: Ask a client what problem they really wanted solved.

author: W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne
text: Instead of fighting in crowded 'red oceans', create uncontested 'blue oceans' with new value.
q: What is a blue ocean?
a: An uncontested market space with new demand.
action: Brainstorm one service nobody locally offers.

author: W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne
text: Eliminate, reduce, raise, create: redesign your offering to cut costs while raising value.
q: What is the ERRC grid?
action: Fill out an ERRC grid for your main service.

author: David Allen
text: Your mind is for having ideas, not holding them. Capture everything in a trusted system.
q: What is the purpose of capturing tasks?
a: To free your mind by storing tasks in a trusted system.
action: Write every open loop on paper today.

author: David Allen
text: If an action takes less than two minutes, do it now.
q: What is GTD's two-minute rule?
a: If it takes under two minutes, do it immediately.
action: Clear all two-minute emails this morning.

author: David Allen
text: Define the next physical action for every project. Vague projects stall; concrete actions move.
q: What keeps projects moving in GTD?
action: Write the next action for each active job.

author: David Allen
text: Do a weekly review: clear inboxes, update lists, look ahead. It keeps the system trustworthy.
q: What is the weekly review?
a: A weekly reset of lists and plans.
action: Do a 30-minute weekly review on Friday.

author: Morgan Housel
text: Doing well with money is more about behaviour than intelligence. Patience and humility beat cleverness.
q: What matters most in managing money, per Housel?
action: Automate one savings transfer today.

author: Morgan Housel
text: Wealth is what you don't see — the cars not bought. Spending to show wealth is the fastest way to lose it.
q: How does Housel define wealth?
action: Delay one purchase meant to impress others.

author: Morgan Housel
text: Room for error is underrated. Leave a margin of safety so bad luck doesn't wipe you out.
q: Why is room for error important?
a: It lets you survive bad luck and stay in the game.
action: Calculate how many months of costs your cash reserve covers.

author: Morgan Housel
text: Compounding works best when uninterrupted. The key is staying in the game a long time.
q: What does compounding need most?
action: Set up a monthly automatic investment, however small.

author: Morgan Housel
text: Enough is a skill. Moving goalposts can lead to risking what you need for what you don't.
q: Why is knowing 'enough' important?
a: Endless wanting leads to reckless risk.
action: Write what 'enough' income means for you.

author: George S. Clason
text: Pay yourself first: keep at least a tenth of all you earn.
q: What is the first cure for a lean purse?
a: Save at least one-tenth of everything you earn.
action: Move 10% of today's income to savings.

author: George S. Clason
text: Make your money work for you: put savings into assets that earn returns.
q: What should saved gold do?
action: Research one investment option for 15 minutes.

author: George S. Clason
text: Guard your treasure from loss: invest only where principal is safe, and seek advice from experts.
q: What does Clason say about risky investments?
a: Protect principal; take advice from the experienced.
action: Ask an experienced person before your next big investment.

author: George S. Clason
text: Control expenses: distinguish necessary expenses from desires, which are endless.
q: Why control expenses?
a: Desires are endless; budgets keep necessities in check.
action: Write a monthly budget for the business.

author: Robert Kiyosaki
text: Assets put money in your pocket; liabilities take money out. Buy assets.
q: How does Kiyosaki define an asset?
a: Something that puts money in your pocket.
action: Classify your big purchases as assets or liabilities.

author: Robert Kiyosaki
text: Financial literacy is essential: learn to read numbers like a balance sheet and cash flow statement.
q: What skill does Kiyosaki emphasise?
action: Read your last month's profit and loss in detail.

author: Robert Kiyosaki
text: Mind your own business: build your asset column while working your job.
q: What does 'mind your own business' mean here?
a: Build your own assets, not just earn wages.
action: Spend an hour on an income-producing asset.

author: Benjamin Graham
text: Mr. Market is moody: his offers swing between euphoria and despair. Use his prices, don't be guided by them.
q: Who is Mr. Market?
a: A metaphor for a moody market offering prices daily.
action: Ignore market news today; check your long-term plan instead.

author: Benjamin Graham
text: Margin of safety: buy only when price is well below value, protecting against mistakes.
q: What is the margin of safety?
a: Buying well below intrinsic value to cushion errors.
action: Apply a safety margin to your next equipment purchase decision.

author: Benjamin Graham
text: The investor's chief problem — and worst enemy — is likely to be himself.
q: What is the investor's worst enemy, per Graham?
action: Write investment rules and follow them without exceptions.

author: John Warrillow
text: A business that depends on its owner is hard to sell. Standardise services and reduce owner dependence.
q: What makes a business sellable, per Warrillow?
a: Standardised offerings that don't depend on the owner.
action: Document one process only you currently know.

author: John Warrillow
text: Specialise in one thing you do well and productise it with a fixed price.
q: What does productising a service mean?
a: Packaging a service with defined scope and fixed price.
action: Create a fixed-price package for a common job.

author: John Warrillow
text: Charge up front or get deposits to improve cash flow.
q: How can service businesses improve cash flow?
action: Add a deposit requirement to your next quote.

author: Simon Sinek
text: People don't buy what you do; they buy why you do it. Lead with purpose, then how and what.
q: What is the Golden Circle?
a: Why, How, What — start with why.
action: Write one sentence about why your company exists.

author: Simon Sinek
