text: Great leaders create a circle of safety where people feel protected and trusted.
q: What is the 'circle of safety'?
a: An environment where people feel safe and trusted.
action: Back up a worker publicly today.

author: Simon Sinek
text: Business is an infinite game: the aim is to keep playing, not to 'win'. Think long-term.
q: What's the goal in an infinite game?
a: To keep playing — long-term survival and growth.
action: Make one decision today with a 10-year view.

author: Kerry Patterson et al.
text: When stakes are high and emotions strong, make it safe to talk. Safety comes before content.
q: What must come first in crucial conversations?
action: Start a difficult talk by stating your good intent.

author: Kerry Patterson et al.
text: Start with heart: ask what you really want for yourself, the other person and the relationship.
q: What does 'start with heart' mean?
a: Clarify what you truly want before speaking.
action: Before a hard talk, write what you want from it.

author: Kerry Patterson et al.
text: Separate facts from stories. We react to the stories we tell ourselves about facts.
q: Why separate facts from stories?
a: We often react to our interpretations, not the facts.
action: Write the facts of a conflict without any judgement words.

author: Patrick Lencioni
book: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
text: Trust is the foundation of teamwork; without vulnerability-based trust, teams avoid conflict.
q: What is the first dysfunction?
action: Admit a mistake to your team today.

author: Patrick Lencioni
book: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
text: Healthy teams have productive conflict over ideas. Artificial harmony hides problems.
q: What does fear of conflict produce?
action: Ask the crew to challenge your plan for tomorrow.

author: Patrick Lencioni
book: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
text: Commitment requires clarity and buy-in; people commit when they've been heard.
q: What enables commitment?
action: End your next meeting by confirming who does what by when.

author: Patrick Lencioni
book: The Five Dysfunctions of a Team
text: Accountability means peers holding each other to standards, not just the boss.
q: Who holds people accountable in strong teams?
action: Set one shared crew standard and ask everyone to uphold it.

author: Patrick Lencioni
text: Ideal team players are humble, hungry and people-smart.
q: What three virtues define an ideal team player?
action: Rate yourself on humble, hungry, smart.

author: John Doerr
text: OKRs: set ambitious Objectives with measurable Key Results that show progress.
q: What are OKRs?
action: Write one OKR for this quarter.

author: John Doerr
text: Key results must be measurable and verifiable; 'it's not a key result unless it has a number'.
q: What defines a good key result?
action: Add a number to one vague goal.

author: Charlie Munger
text: Invert, always invert: ask what would guarantee failure, then avoid it.
q: What is inversion?
a: Thinking about what would cause failure and avoiding it.
action: List three things that would ruin your business. Avoid them.

author: Charlie Munger
text: Build a latticework of mental models from many disciplines to think better.
q: What is a latticework of mental models?
a: Key ideas from many disciplines used together.
action: Learn one new mental model this week.

author: Charlie Munger
text: Stay within your circle of competence: know what you know and what you don't.
q: What is the circle of competence?
a: The area where you truly have expertise.
action: Decline one job outside your competence or partner with an expert.

author: Charlie Munger
text: Show me the incentive and I'll show you the outcome. Incentives drive behaviour.
q: What did Munger say about incentives?
action: Check whether your pay system rewards the behaviour you want.

author: Warren Buffett
text: It takes 20 years to build a reputation and five minutes to ruin it.
q: How long does it take to ruin a reputation?
action: Fix one small thing that could hurt your reputation.

author: Warren Buffett
text: Be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful.
q: What is Buffett's contrarian rule?
a: Fearful when others are greedy; greedy when others are fearful.
action: Note where others are panicking in your market and look for opportunity.

author: Warren Buffett
text: Look for businesses with a moat: a durable competitive advantage.
q: What is an economic moat?
action: Name your company's moat and how to widen it.

author: Dan Martell
text: Hire to buy back your time: delegate tasks below your hourly value.
q: What is the buyback principle?
a: Hire to free time for higher-value work.
action: Calculate your hourly value and delegate one task below it.

author: Dan Martell
text: Use the camcorder method: record yourself doing a task to make it easy to delegate.
q: What is the camcorder method?
a: Recording a task to create training material.
action: Film yourself doing one admin task.

author: Chet Holmes
text: Pigheaded discipline: master a few key skills through repetition rather than doing 4,000 things.
q: What does Holmes call the key trait?
action: Practise your sales pitch five times.

author: Chet Holmes
text: Educate prospects: share useful market data that positions you as the expert.
q: What is education-based marketing?
a: Sharing valuable information to attract buyers.
action: Post a short tip about drainage or groundwork online.

author: Neil Rackham
text: Ask Situation, Problem, Implication and Need-payoff questions to uncover real needs.
q: What does SPIN stand for?
action: Use SPIN questions at your next site visit.

author: Neil Rackham
text: Implication questions reveal the cost of the problem, making solutions valuable.
q: What do implication questions do?
action: Ask a client 'What happens if the water keeps pooling?'

author: Geoff Smart & Randy Street
text: Hiring mistakes are costly; use a scorecard of outcomes before interviewing.
q: What should you create before hiring?
a: A scorecard of outcomes and competencies.
action: Write a scorecard for your next hire.

author: Geoff Smart & Randy Street
text: Use a chronological interview: walk through every job, asking about successes, failures and why they left.
q: What is the topgrading interview?
a: A chronological walk through the candidate's career.
action: Prepare five chronological questions for your next interview.

author: Josh Kaufman
text: Every business has five parts: value creation, marketing, sales, value delivery, finance.
q: What are the five parts of every business?
a: Value creation, marketing, sales, delivery, finance.
action: Rate each of the five in your company.

author: Josh Kaufman
text: Pricing is based on value to the customer, not just your costs.
q: How should prices be set?
a: Based on value to the customer.
action: Estimate the value your work creates for a client.

author: Phil Knight
text: Just keep going. Knight's story shows persistence through setbacks and cash crunches.
q: What lesson runs through Shoe Dog?
action: Make the next move on a project that stalled.

author: Phil Knight
text: Cash flow can kill a growing company. Growth uses cash before it returns it.
q: Why can growth be dangerous?
a: It consumes cash before returning it.
action: Check your cash flow forecast for the next three months.

author: Sam Walton
text: Exceed customer expectations. If you do, they'll come back again and again.
q: What did Walton say keeps customers coming back?
action: Do one unexpected extra on a job this week.

author: Sam Walton
text: Control expenses better than competitors. Frugality is a competitive advantage.
q: How did Walton gain advantage?
a: By controlling costs better than competitors.
action: Review fuel and machine costs for waste.

author: Ray Dalio
text: Pain + reflection = progress. Mistakes are opportunities to learn.
q: What is Dalio's formula for progress?
action: Write a lesson from one recent failure.

author: Ray Dalio
text: Radical transparency: share honest feedback openly so the best ideas win.
q: What is radical transparency?
a: Open, honest sharing of information and feedback.
action: Ask the crew for brutally honest feedback on your leadership.

author: Ray Dalio
text: Write your principles down so decisions become consistent and teachable.
q: Why write principles down?
action: Write three principles for running your business.

author: Kim Scott
text: Care personally and challenge directly. Kindness without honesty is ruinous empathy.
q: What is radical candor?
action: Give specific, kind but direct feedback today.

author: Kim Scott
text: Praise in public, criticise in private.
q: Where should criticism be given?
action: Praise a crew member publicly today.

author: Marshall Goldsmith
book: What Got You Here Won't Get You There
text: Habits that brought success may block the next level. Stop adding too much value to others' ideas.
q: What is the problem with past success?
a: Old habits may block future growth.
action: Let someone's idea stand without improving it.

author: Marshall Goldsmith
text: Ask daily active questions: 'Did I do my best to…?' to measure effort, not outcomes.
q: What are active questions?
a: Questions measuring effort: 'Did I do my best to…?'
action: Write three 'Did I do my best to…' questions for tonight.

author: Stephen M. R. Covey
text: Trust increases speed and lowers cost. Low trust adds a tax to every transaction.
q: How does trust affect business?
a: High trust increases speed and lowers costs.
action: Keep every small promise to clients this week.

author: Michael Porter
text: There are three generic strategies: cost leadership, differentiation and focus. Being stuck in the middle is dangerous.
q: What are Porter's three generic strategies?
action: Decide which of the three strategies your company follows.

author: Michael Porter
text: Five forces shape profitability: rivals, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power and supplier power.
q: Name Porter's five forces.
a: Rivalry, new entrants, substitutes, buyer power, supplier power.
action: Note which force squeezes your margins most.

author: Michael Porter
text: Strategy is choosing what not to do. Trade-offs make a position hard to copy.
q: What is the essence of strategy, per Porter?
action: Name one customer type you will stop serving.

author: Al Ries & Jack Trout
text: Positioning happens in the customer's mind. Own one simple word or idea in their head.
q: Where does positioning happen?
action: Pick one word you want customers to associate with you.

author: Al Ries & Jack Trout
text: It's better to be first than better. If you can't be first in a category, create a new one.
q: What is the Law of Leadership?
action: Find a sub-category you could be first in locally.

author: Al Ries & Jack Trout
text: The Law of Focus: owning a single word, like 'safety', is the most powerful marketing concept.
q: What is the Law of Focus?
a: Own one word in the prospect's mind.
action: Use your chosen word in all your marketing this month.

author: Seth Godin
text: Be remarkable. Safe, ordinary products are invisible; only remarkable ones get talked about.
q: What is a 'purple cow'?
action: Add one remarkable touch to how you finish jobs.

author: Seth Godin
text: Find the smallest viable audience and serve them deeply.
q: What is the smallest viable audience?
a: The minimum group you can serve exceptionally well.
action: Describe your ideal customer in one paragraph.

author: Seth Godin
text: Most worthwhile pursuits have a 'dip' — a hard slog. Quit the wrong things fast, and push through the dip on the right ones.
q: What is the Dip?
a: The difficult period between starting and mastering.
action: Decide whether one struggle is a dip worth pushing through.

author: Seth Godin
text: Be indispensable: bring art, judgement and generosity to your work.
q: What makes someone a linchpin?
a: Being indispensable through creativity and judgement.
action: Do one task today with extra care no one asked for.

author: Donald Miller
text: Make the customer the hero and your business the guide. Customers care about their story.
q: In StoryBrand, who is the hero?
action: Rewrite your website headline around the customer's problem.

author: Donald Miller
text: Give customers a simple plan: three clear steps to working with you.
q: What simple element reduces customer confusion?
action: Write your three steps: call, site visit, job done.

author: Gary Vaynerchuk
text: Give value repeatedly (jabs) before asking for the sale (right hook).
q: What does the boxing metaphor mean?
a: Provide value repeatedly before asking for a sale.
action: Post a helpful tip before posting any promotion.

author: Allan Dib
text: Marketing has three phases: before (prospect), during (lead) and after (customer). Plan each.
q: What are the three phases?
action: Plan one follow-up step for after each job.

author: Allan Dib
text: Nurture leads with follow-up; most sales happen after multiple contacts.
q: Why follow up repeatedly?
action: Follow up on three unanswered quotes today.

author: Frank Bettger
book: How I Raised Myself from Failure to Success in Selling
text: Enthusiasm is contagious. Act enthusiastic and you'll become enthusiastic.
q: What did Bettger say about enthusiasm?
a: Acting enthusiastic makes you enthusiastic, and it's contagious.
action: Bring visible enthusiasm to your next client call.

author: Frank Bettger
book: How I Raised Myself from Failure to Success in Selling
text: Keep records of calls and results; numbers reveal what each call is worth.
q: Why track sales calls?
a: To know your conversion rates and value per call.
action: Track how many quotes you send this week and how many win.

author: Zig Ziglar
text: You can have everything you want if you help enough other people get what they want.
q: What is Ziglar's core principle?
a: Help others get what they want and you'll get what you want.
action: Focus a sales talk entirely on the client's goals.

author: Jeffrey Gitomer
book: The Little Red Book of Selling
text: People love to buy but hate being sold. Create an atmosphere where they want to buy.
q: What do people hate?
action: Ask questions instead of pitching at your next site visit.

author: Jeffrey Gitomer
book: The Little Red Book of Selling
text: Your reputation precedes your sales call. Referrals are the easiest sales.
q: What are the easiest sales?
action: Ask a satisfied client for one referral.

author: Brian Tracy
text: The top 20% of salespeople earn 80% of the income, mainly by prospecting more and better.
q: What separates top salespeople?
action: Spend one hour prospecting new clients this week.

author: Daniel Pink
text: Everyone is in sales now: persuading, influencing, moving others.
q: What is Pink's main claim?
a: Most of us are in sales — moving others.
action: Notice how many times you 'sell' today.

author: Daniel Pink
text: Motivation for complex work comes from autonomy, mastery and purpose, not carrots and sticks.
q: What three elements drive motivation?
action: Give a worker more say in how they do a task.

author: Daniel Pink
text: Timing matters: most people peak in the morning for analytic work. Schedule hard tasks accordingly.
q: When are most people sharpest analytically?
action: Do quoting and pricing in your peak hours.

author: Ken Blanchard & Spencer Johnson
text: Set one-minute goals, give one-minute praisings and one-minute redirects.
q: What are the three secrets of the One Minute Manager?
action: Give one specific one-minute praising today.

author: Ken Blanchard & Spencer Johnson
text: Catch people doing something right.
q: What should managers look for?
action: Catch a worker doing something right and say it.

author: Spencer Johnson
text: Change happens; anticipate it, adapt quickly, and enjoy the new.
q: What's the main lesson of 'Who Moved My Cheese'?
a: Anticipate and adapt to change quickly.
action: Name one market change and plan your adaptation.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Let the other person feel the idea is theirs. People support what they help create.
q: Why let others own ideas?
a: People support ideas they feel are their own.
action: Ask your crew how to solve a problem rather than telling them.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Call attention to mistakes indirectly, and talk about your own mistakes first.
q: How should mistakes be pointed out?
action: Share a past mistake before correcting someone.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Give people a fine reputation to live up to.
q: What does a fine reputation do?
a: Gives people a standard to live up to.
action: Tell a worker you know they take pride in quality.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Begin in a friendly way. A drop of honey catches more flies than a gallon of gall.
q: How should you begin when you want agreement?
action: Open a tough email with a friendly line.

author: Dale Carnegie
book: How to Win Friends and Influence People
text: Get the other person saying 'yes, yes' immediately. Early agreement builds momentum.
q: What is the 'yes, yes' technique?
a: Start with questions the other will agree with.
action: Begin a negotiation with points you both agree on.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People
text: Production vs production capability (P/PC balance): don't kill the goose that lays golden eggs.
q: What is the P/PC balance?
a: Balancing results with maintaining the capacity to produce them.
action: Schedule maintenance on your main machine.

author: Stephen Covey
text: Find your voice and inspire others to find theirs.
q: What is the 8th habit?
a: Find your voice and help others find theirs.
action: Ask a worker what they're passionate about.

author: Napoleon Hill
text: Form a mastermind group: two or more people working in harmony toward a goal.
q: What is a mastermind?
a: A group of people cooperating toward a goal.
action: Invite two other business owners for a monthly coffee.

author: Napoleon Hill
text: Persistence is the sustained effort necessary to induce faith. Most people quit just before success.
q: What does Hill say most people lack?
action: Keep going on one project despite a setback.

author: Napoleon Hill
text: Specialised knowledge, organised and applied, is power.
q: What kind of knowledge is power, per Hill?
a: Specialised knowledge applied with a plan.
action: Learn one regulation that affects your trade.

author: Napoleon Hill
text: Decision: successful people decide quickly and change slowly; failures do the opposite.
q: How do successful people make decisions?
action: Make a quick decision on something you've been dithering on.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: 'Beware of little expenses; a small leak will sink a great ship.'
q: What did Franklin warn about little expenses?
action: Find one small recurring cost to cut.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: 'Remember that time is money.' Idle hours carry real cost.
q: What did Franklin equate with money?
action: Calculate what a wasted crew hour costs you.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Credit is money; pay debts punctually, and your reputation lets you borrow when needed.
q: Why pay debts punctually?
action: Pay one supplier invoice early.

author: Sun Tzu
text: All warfare is based on deception — in business, keep plans private until ready.
q: What is the basis of warfare, per Sun Tzu?
action: Keep a new plan private until it's ready.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Speed is the essence of war. Act quickly on opportunities before others react.
q: What is the essence of war?
action: Reply to a new enquiry within one hour today.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Attack where the enemy is unprepared. Serve needs competitors neglect.
q: Where should you attack?
action: Find a service competitors do badly and do it well.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Treat your soldiers as your children and they will follow you into the deepest valleys.
q: How should leaders treat their people?
a: With care, like their own children.
action: Do something to make the crew's work more comfortable.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Plan carefully: the general who wins makes many calculations before battle.
q: What precedes victory?
action: Calculate costs carefully before your next quote.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Do not develop a favourite weapon. Over-attachment to one tool limits you.
q: Why avoid a favourite weapon?
action: Learn to use a tool or method you avoid.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Become acquainted with every art. Breadth makes your craft wiser.
q: What should a warrior know?
action: Spend 15 minutes learning about bookkeeping or law.

author: Miyamoto Musashi
text: Know the rhythm of things: timing in business, like in combat, decides outcomes.
q: Why is rhythm important to Musashi?
action: Time a price increase for the start of your busy season.

author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: It is better to be feared than loved if you cannot be both — but never be hated.
q: What must a leader avoid above all?
action: Make sure discipline is fair and consistent.

author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: Inflict harm all at once, but grant benefits gradually so they are savoured.
q: How should benefits be given, per Machiavelli?
action: Deliver bad news in one go; spread rewards over time.

author: Niccolò Machiavelli
text: Change creates enemies among those who did well under the old order, and only lukewarm support from those who might benefit.
q: Why is introducing change hard?
a: Old beneficiaries oppose it; new ones only weakly support it.
action: Plan how to win support before a change at work.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Avoid outshining the master. Superiority provokes resentment.
q: Why avoid outshining superiors?
action: Let a key client take credit for a good idea.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Never promise more than you can deliver. Hopes betrayed are long remembered.
q: What does Gracián say about promises?
a: Don't promise more than you can deliver.
action: Set realistic completion dates in your next quote.

author: Baltasar Gracián
text: Choose your associates well; you're judged by the company you keep.
q: How are we judged, per Gracián?
action: Review one subcontractor's reputation.

author: Samuel Smiles
text: Business success depends on attention, application, accuracy, method, punctuality and dispatch.
q: Which qualities did Smiles say business needs?
a: Attention, application, accuracy, method, punctuality, dispatch.
action: Be five minutes early to every appointment today.

author: Samuel Smiles
text: Small savings, steadily made, are the foundation of independence.
q: What is the basis of independence, per Smiles?
action: Save a small fixed amount today.

author: Samuel Smiles
text: Debt makes a man a slave; avoid borrowing for consumption.
q: What did Smiles say about debt?
action: Pay down one small debt.

author: Verne Harnish
text: Every growing firm must master four decisions: people, strategy, execution and cash.
q: What are the four Scaling Up decisions?
action: Score yourself 1–10 on each of the four.

author: Verne Harnish
text: Hold a short daily huddle: what's up, key numbers, where you're stuck.
q: What is a daily huddle?
a: A 5–15 minute team check-in on progress and blockers.
action: Hold a 10-minute morning huddle with the crew.

author: Verne Harnish
text: Cash is oxygen. Shorten the cash conversion cycle: invoice faster, collect sooner.
q: What does Harnish call cash?
action: Send every outstanding invoice today.

author: Keith Cunningham
text: Schedule thinking time: sit with one important question and a notepad, undisturbed.
q: What practice does Cunningham recommend?
action: Sit for 30 minutes with one question about your business.

author: Keith Cunningham
text: Avoiding dumb mistakes beats chasing brilliant moves. Stupid tax is expensive.
q: What is the 'dumb tax'?
action: List the costliest avoidable mistake from last year and a rule to prevent it.

author: Keith Cunningham
text: Know your numbers: revenue, gross margin, overhead and cash. Ignorance of numbers is the most common killer.
q: What must every owner know?
action: Calculate your gross margin on last month's jobs.

author: Ramit Sethi
book: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
text: Spend extravagantly on what you love and cut costs mercilessly on what you don't.
q: What is conscious spending?
a: Spend big on what you love; cut what you don't care about.
action: Cut one expense you don't value.

author: Ramit Sethi
book: I Will Teach You to Be Rich
text: Automate your finances so saving and investing happen without willpower.
q: Why automate finances?
a: It removes willpower from saving and investing.
action: Set up an automatic savings transfer on payday.

author: Thomas Stanley
text: Most millionaires live below their means, drive used cars and budget carefully.
q: How do most millionaires live?
action: Compare your lifestyle spending with your income.

author: Thomas Stanley
text: Wealth is built by allocating time, energy and money efficiently toward building wealth.
q: What three resources do wealthy people allocate efficiently?
action: Spend 30 minutes planning your finances.

author: Nassim Taleb
text: Some things gain from disorder. Build a business that benefits from shocks: diverse clients, low debt, options.
q: What does antifragile mean?
action: Reduce dependence on your single biggest client.

author: Nassim Taleb
text: Rare, high-impact events shape history. Prepare for what you can't predict.
q: What is a Black Swan?
action: Ensure you have insurance and reserves for a bad surprise.

author: Nassim Taleb
text: Don't trust advice from people who don't bear the consequences.
q: What does skin in the game mean?
a: Bearing the consequences of your decisions.
action: Ask advisers whether they have done what they recommend.

author: Annie Duke
text: Judge decisions by process, not outcome. Good decisions can have bad results.
q: What is 'resulting'?
a: Judging decision quality solely by outcome.
action: Review a decision based on what you knew then.

author: Annie Duke
text: Quitting at the right time is a skill. Set kill criteria in advance.
q: What are kill criteria?
a: Pre-set conditions for when to quit.
action: Set a kill criterion for one struggling service.

author: Shane Parrish
text: Most bad decisions happen in ordinary moments when emotion, ego or social pressure take over. Create space before reacting.
q: When do most bad decisions happen?
a: In ordinary moments when defaults take over.
action: Pause before replying to an annoying message.

author: Robert Greene
text: Mastery requires an apprenticeship phase of deep, patient practice under good mentors.
q: What is the first phase of mastery?
action: Ask an experienced tradesperson to teach you a technique.

author: Robert Greene
text: Guard your reputation with your life; it is the cornerstone of power.
q: What should be guarded at all costs?
action: Address one complaint before it spreads.

author: Robert Greene
text: Create a sense of urgency: work as if you're down to your last resources.
q: What is the 'death-ground' strategy?
a: Creating urgency as if no retreat is possible.
action: Set a hard deadline on a task you've delayed.

author: Ryan Holiday
text: Ego sabotages learning. Stay a student, especially after success.
q: What is the enemy, per Holiday?
action: Ask for feedback after your next successful job.

author: Ryan Holiday
text: Perception, action, will: see clearly, act decisively, endure what you can't change.
q: What are the three disciplines?
action: Apply the three to today's biggest problem.

author: Ryan Holiday
text: Stillness — calm focus — is the key to great performance in business and life.
q: What does Holiday call the key?
action: Take a 10-minute walk without your phone.

author: Ryan Holiday
text: Self-discipline in small things — sleep, food, words — builds the capacity for big ones.
q: What does Holiday say discipline determines?
action: Keep one small promise to yourself today.

author: Tim Ferriss
text: Eliminate before you automate, automate before you delegate.
q: What is the order of operations?
action: Eliminate one recurring task this week.

author: Tim Ferriss
text: Batch similar tasks: check email and do admin at set times.
q: What is batching?
a: Grouping similar tasks to do at once.
action: Answer emails only twice today.

author: Tim Ferriss
text: Fear-setting: define your worst case, how to prevent and repair it, and the cost of inaction.
q: What is fear-setting?
a: Defining fears, prevention, repair, and cost of inaction.
action: Do a fear-setting exercise on one decision.

author: Darren Hardy
text: Small, smart choices plus consistency plus time equal radical difference.
q: What is the compound effect formula?
a: Small choices + consistency + time = big results.
action: Track one small habit daily for a week.

author: Darren Hardy
text: Track everything you want to improve — money, time, habits. Awareness changes behaviour.
q: Why track behaviour?
action: Track every expense for one day.

author: Grant Cardone
text: Set targets ten times higher than you think and take ten times the action. Most people underestimate effort.
q: What is the 10X Rule?
action: Double your outreach today.

author: Brian Tracy
text: Write goals down, set deadlines and make a plan. Written goals are far more likely to be achieved.
q: What makes goals more effective?
a: Writing them down with deadlines and plans.
action: Write three business goals with dates.

author: Og Mandino
book: The Greatest Salesman in the World
text: Form good habits and become their slave. Persist until you succeed.
q: What did the scroll say to persist until?
action: Make one more sales call than usual.

author: Og Mandino
book: The Greatest Salesman in the World
text: Greet each day with love in your heart; it disarms resistance.
q: How should you greet each day?
action: Greet every client today warmly.

author: Les McKeown
text: Growing firms move through stages: early struggle, fun, whitewater, then predictable success. Systems are needed in whitewater.
q: What stage requires systems?
action: Write one system to reduce chaos in your busiest week.

author: Michael Gerber
text: Contractors must price for overhead, profit and their own wage; most underprice.
q: What do most contractors forget in pricing?
action: Recalculate your hourly rate including overhead and profit.

author: Michael Gerber
text: A good job file includes scope, schedule, materials, risks and photos.
q: What makes a good job file?
action: Create a job file template.

author: Jack Stack
text: Open-book management: teach employees the numbers and let them share in success.
q: What is open-book management?
a: Sharing financial data and rewarding results with employees.
action: Show your crew the cost of one job.

author: Jack Welch
text: Candour is crucial. Telling the truth fast speeds everything up.
q: What did Welch say is most crucial?
action: Give one straight answer you've been softening.

author: Jack Welch
text: Differentiate: reward top performers, develop the middle and deal with low performers.
q: What is differentiation?
action: Reward your best worker visibly.

author: Ed Catmull
text: Early ideas are ugly babies; protect them while they mature.
q: What are 'ugly babies'?
action: Give a new idea a chance before judging it.

author: Ed Catmull
text: Candid feedback groups ('braintrusts') improve work without taking ownership.
q: What is a braintrust?
a: A group giving candid, non-binding feedback.
action: Ask peers to critique a job plan.

author: Howard Schultz
text: Treat employees as partners; their engagement shapes the customer experience.
q: How did Schultz treat employees?
action: Thank a worker for their contribution today.

author: Ray Kroc
text: Press on: nothing takes the place of persistence.
q: What did Kroc champion?
action: Finish an unfinished task.

author: Elon Musk biography (Isaacson)
text: Question every requirement, delete parts, simplify, accelerate, then automate.
q: What is 'the algorithm'?
action: Question one requirement in a current process.

author: Bob Iger
text: Optimism, courage, focus, decisiveness, curiosity, fairness, thoughtfulness, authenticity, perfection and integrity guide leadership.
q: Name three of Iger's leadership principles.
action: Act on one principle today.

author: Satya Nadella
text: Growth mindset culture: be a learn-it-all, not a know-it-all.
q: What does Nadella prefer to a know-it-all?
action: Learn one new thing from a crew member.

author: Carol Dweck
text: A growth mindset believes abilities can be developed. It welcomes challenge.
q: What is a growth mindset?
a: Belief that abilities can be developed.
action: Try a challenging task you've avoided.

author: Angela Duckworth
text: Grit — passion and perseverance for long-term goals — predicts success more than talent.
q: What is grit?
action: Commit to one long-term goal.

author: Charles Duhigg
text: Habits follow a loop: cue, routine, reward. Change the routine while keeping cue and reward.
q: What is the habit loop?
action: Identify the cue of one bad habit.

author: Charles Duhigg
text: Keystone habits, like exercise or planning, trigger widespread positive change.
q: What is a keystone habit?
a: A habit that sparks other positive changes.
action: Start one keystone habit.

author: Nir Eyal
text: Distraction is an escape from discomfort. Master internal triggers to stay focused.
q: What causes distraction, per Eyal?
action: Note what feeling precedes your phone checking.

author: Brené Brown
text: Clear is kind; unclear is unkind. Vague expectations hurt people.
q: What does 'clear is kind' mean?
a: Clear expectations are kinder than vague ones.
action: Clarify expectations with one worker.

author: Simon Sinek
text: People inspired by why stay loyal through hard times.
q: Why do purpose-driven firms have loyal customers?
action: Tell a client why you care about quality.

author: Patrick Bet-David
text: Know yourself, then think five moves ahead, like a chess master.
q: What does Bet-David urge?
action: Plan your next five business moves.

author: Robert Kiyosaki
text: Income comes from four quadrants: employee, self-employed, business owner, investor.
q: What are the four quadrants?
action: Identify your quadrant and your next one.

author: MJ DeMarco
text: Wealth comes from control, entry barriers, need, time and scale — not from slow saving alone.
q: What are DeMarco's CENTS?
action: Rate your business on CENTS.

author: Paul Jarvis
text: Growth isn't always better; staying small and profitable can be the goal.
q: What does Jarvis question?
a: The assumption that growth is always good.
action: Decide your ideal company size.

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Grow your best customers like prize pumpkins; cut the worst.
q: What is the Pumpkin Plan?
a: Focus on top clients and cut poor ones.
action: Rank your clients and drop the worst one.

author: Jim Collins
text: Technology accelerates momentum but never creates it. Adopt tools that fit your core, not fads.
q: How do great companies treat technology?
a: As an accelerator, not a creator, of momentum.
action: Pick one tool that would speed up your best service.

author: Jim Collins
text: Decline begins with hubris born of success, then undisciplined pursuit of more.
q: What is the first stage of decline?
action: List one assumption you've stopped questioning since things went well.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: The client sees your business, not you. Every touchpoint — phone, truck, site — tells a story.
q: What do customers experience, per Gerber?
action: Clean the truck and tidy the site sign today.

author: Michael E. Gerber
text: Quantify everything: how many calls, quotes, wins. Numbers make the invisible visible.
q: Why quantify, per Gerber?
action: Count this week's calls, quotes and wins.

author: Eric Ries
text: Ask 'five whys' to find the root cause of a problem, then fix the system.
q: What is the five whys technique?
a: Asking why five times to reach a root cause.
action: Ask five whys about a recent delay on site.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Effective people make few, fundamental decisions rather than many small ones.
q: What kind of decisions do effective executives make?
action: Turn a recurring decision into a standing rule.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Use feedback analysis: write expected results of decisions, then compare 9–12 months later.
q: What is feedback analysis?
a: Comparing actual results to written expectations.
action: Write expected results for one decision today.

author: Peter Drucker
text: Know how you learn and work best — reader or listener, alone or in teams.
q: What should you know about yourself?
a: How you perform and learn best.
action: Note when and how you work best.

author: Andrew Grove
text: Detect problems at the lowest-value stage. Inspect early when fixing is cheap.
q: Where should problems be caught?
action: Check measurements before the concrete truck arrives.

author: Andrew Grove
text: Use leading indicators to see the future: quotes sent today predict revenue next month.
q: What are leading indicators?
action: Track quotes sent this week as a leading indicator.

author: Robert Cialdini
text: Unity: people say yes to those they see as part of 'us'. Shared identity is powerful.
q: What is the unity principle?
action: Mention your local roots to a local client.

author: Chris Voss
text: Use an accusation audit: name every negative thing they might think about you before they say it.
q: What is an accusation audit?
a: Listing the other side's possible negative feelings upfront.
action: Start a price talk: 'You may think this is expensive…'

author: Chris Voss
text: The late-night FM DJ voice — calm, slow, downward — calms tension.
q: What voice does Voss recommend?
a: A calm, slow 'late-night FM DJ' voice.
action: Use a slower, calmer voice on a tense call.

author: Cal Newport
text: Do fewer things, work at a natural pace and obsess over quality.
q: What are the three principles of slow productivity?
a: Fewer things, natural pace, obsess over quality.
action: Limit active jobs to what you can do excellently.

author: Cal Newport
text: Replace ad-hoc messaging with clear processes; inbox chaos kills focus.
q: What does Newport propose instead of constant messaging?
action: Create a standard form for job enquiries.

author: Greg McKeown
text: Make the essential easy: ask 'what if this could be easy?'
q: What question does Effortless pose?
a: What if this could be easy?
action: Simplify one hard recurring task.

author: Eliyahu Goldratt
text: Reduce batch sizes to speed flow; huge batches create waiting.
q: What do large batches cause?
action: Split a big order into smaller deliveries.

author: Gino Wickman
text: Every role should have one clear measurable that shows if the job is done well.
q: What does each seat need?
action: Give each crew role one clear measure.

author: Gino Wickman
text: Every company needs a Visionary and an Integrator who turns vision into execution.
q: What two roles does Rocket Fuel describe?
action: Decide who in your company is the integrator.

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Pay yourself a fair salary; an owner working for free is subsidising an unprofitable business.
q: Why must the owner be paid?
a: Otherwise the business is hiding losses.
action: Set a regular owner's pay transfer.

author: Mike Michalowicz
text: Fix needs in order: sales, profit, order, impact, legacy — like a business pyramid.
q: What is the Business Hierarchy of Needs?
action: Find the lowest unmet level and fix it.

author: Alex Hormozi
text: Stack bonuses that solve the next problems the customer will face.
q: How should bonuses be chosen?
a: To solve the customer's next problems.
action: Add a free drainage check to your landscaping offer.

author: Alex Hormozi
text: Volume negates luck: do more outreach than seems reasonable.
q: What negates luck in lead generation?
action: Make 20 contacts this week.

author: Jocko Willink
text: Leaders must balance opposites: confident not cocky, disciplined not rigid.
q: What is the dichotomy of leadership?
action: Find one area where you overcorrect.

author: Jocko Willink
text: Decentralised command: give small teams clear intent and let them lead.
q: What is decentralised command?
a: Empowering junior leaders with clear intent.
action: Let a foreman run tomorrow's job.

author: Ben Horowitz
book: What You Do Is Who You Are
text: Culture is what people do when the leader isn't there.
q: What is culture, per Horowitz?
action: Ask what happens on site when you're absent.

author: Jason Fried & DHH
book: It Doesn't Have to Be Crazy at Work
text: Calm companies set reasonable hours and deadlines; chaos isn't a badge of honour.
q: What do calm companies avoid?
action: Set a firm end time for workdays this week.

author: Daniel Kahneman
text: Different people judge the same case differently; checklists and guidelines reduce noise.
q: What is noise in judgement?
action: Create a quote checklist so prices are consistent.

author: Morgan Housel
text: Things that never change: risk, greed, fear, incentives. Plan around timeless behaviour.
q: What does Housel focus on in Same as Ever?
action: Plan for a downturn, since cycles always return.

author: Warren Buffett
text: Rule No. 1: never lose money. Rule No. 2: never forget rule No. 1.
q: What are Buffett's two rules?
a: Never lose money; never forget rule 1.
action: Check that every job is priced to profit.

author: Warren Buffett
text: Price is what you pay; value is what you get.
q: What is the difference between price and value?
a: Price is paid; value is received.
action: Explain value, not price, in your next quote.

author: Charlie Munger
text: Avoid envy, resentment and self-pity — they are wealth killers.
q: What did Munger say to avoid?
action: Drop one envious thought about a competitor.

author: Ray Dalio
text: Believability-weight decisions: give more weight to people with track records.
q: What is believability weighting?
action: Ask the most experienced person before deciding.

author: Kim Scott
text: Get feedback before giving it: ask 'What could I do that would make it easier to work with me?'
q: How should leaders start with feedback?
action: Ask a worker what you could do better.

author: Stephen M. R. Covey
text: Talk straight, show respect, create transparency and keep commitments.
q: Name two trust behaviours.
action: Be transparent about a job delay.

author: Simon Sinek
text: In great teams, leaders sacrifice their comfort for their people.
q: Why do leaders 'eat last'?
a: They put their people's needs first.
action: Let the crew go home first today.

author: Josh Kaufman
text: Every offer carries perceived risk; reduce it with guarantees and proof.
q: How do you reduce perceived risk?
action: Add before/after photos to quotes.

author: Josh Kaufman
text: Track your sales funnel: prospects → leads → quotes → customers.
q: What is a sales funnel?
a: The stages from prospect to customer.
action: Draw your funnel with last month's numbers.

author: Seth Godin
text: Winners quit fast and often — just not the right things.
q: What do winners do, per Godin?
action: Quit one dead-end effort.

author: Donald Miller
text: Value-driven professionals solve problems, take ownership and get things done.
q: What characterises a value-driven professional?
action: Solve one problem without being asked.

author: Brian Tracy
text: Self-discipline is the key to personal greatness; do what you should when you should.
q: What is the key to greatness, per Tracy?
action: Do one task the moment it's due.

author: Napoleon Hill
text: Desire backed by a definite plan and burning commitment turns into riches.
q: What starts riches, per Hill?
action: Write a burning desire and plan.

author: Tony Robbins
text: Know your numbers: how much you need for security, independence and freedom.
q: What financial dreams does Robbins define?
action: Calculate the income you need for security.

author: Dave Ramsey
text: Build an emergency fund, then pay debts smallest to largest — the debt snowball.

author: Dave Ramsey

action: Share one profit number with the team.

author: Marshall Goldsmith

author: Brian Tracy

action: Rank today's tasks A–E.

action: Make an @phone list and clear it.

action: Track one habit with a check mark.

author: Ryan Holiday
text: The first rule of business: don't make the problem worse.

action: Pause before reacting to a site problem.

action: Keep reserves safe and try one small new venture.

author: Annie Duke

action: Rate your confidence in a forecast.

author: Shane Parrish

action: Visit a site before relying on the drawing.

author: Shane Parrish

action: Ask 'and then what?' about a decision.

author: Shane Parrish

action: Rebuild a price from first principles.

action: Send a short progress photo to a client during a job.

action: Try the opposite approach to a problem.

action: Make your phone number clear on every vehicle.

action: Read for 30 minutes.

author: Jim Rohn

action: List your five and assess.

text: Discipline weighs ounces, regret weighs tons.

action: Choose discipline in one moment.

author: Zig Ziglar
text: Motivation doesn't last; neither does bathing — that's why we recommend it daily.

action: Start with an inspiring read.

author: Earl Nightingale

author: Dale Carnegie

action: Do practical work when you worry.

action: Place three big rocks in tomorrow's calendar.

text: Paradigm shifts change how we see everything; change the lens before the behaviour.

action: View a problem from the customer's lens.

action: Start or join a group of local business owners.

author: Benjamin Franklin

action: Work an extra hour on income today.

author: Seneca

action: Find calm where you are today instead of wishing to be elsewhere.

author: Seneca
text: Count each day as a separate life. Close it at night with a review, as if it were complete.

action: Review today tonight as if it were your whole life.

author: Seneca

action: Tell a trusted friend something real.

author: Seneca

action: Apply one idea instead of quoting it.

author: Seneca

action: Write where you're heading this year.

author: Seneca
text: Avoid the crowd; it sweeps you along into its vices. Spend time with those who improve you.

action: Skip one gathering that drains you.

author: Seneca
text: Restlessness comes from dissatisfaction with oneself. Settle into useful work.

action: Commit an hour to useful work without switching.

author: Seneca
text: Fire tests gold; misfortune tests brave men. Hardship is training.

action: Treat a hardship today as a training exercise.

author: Seneca
text: Look at yourself in a mirror when angry; the ugliness may shame you into calm.

action: Notice your face when irritated.

author: Seneca
text: Hold every day as if it were your last, and you will never fear tomorrow.

author: Seneca

action: Name what you already have enough of.

action: Spend five minutes in quiet reflection.

author: Marcus Aurelius

action: Do one good deed anonymously.

author: Marcus Aurelius

action: Show appreciation to someone you see daily.

action: Do one thing for your community.

author: Marcus Aurelius

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Loss is nothing else but change, and change is nature's delight.

action: Reframe a loss as change.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not act as if you had ten thousand years to live. Death hangs over you; be good while you can.
q: Why act now?
action: Do the good thing you've postponed.

author: Marcus Aurelius

action: Avoid checking others' social media today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Kindness is invincible, if it is sincere. It disarms the most violent person.

action: Respond to hostility with kindness.

author: Marcus Aurelius

action: Remind yourself this morning that no one can harm your character.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The art of living is more like wrestling than dancing; be ready to stand firm.
q: What is the art of living like?
action: Stand firm on one decision today.

author: Marcus Aurelius

q: How did Marcus view correction?
action: Thank someone who corrects you.

author: Epictetus

action: Name one fault honestly.

action: Practise patience with something you want.

author: Epictetus

action: Play your role well today, whatever it is.

action: Respond to criticism with good humour.

action: Think through one decision fully.

author: Epictetus

action: Practise patience in small annoyances.

action: Change one personal habit.

q: What is life like, per Watts?
a: Music — the point is the playing.
action: Enjoy the process of a task.

author: Joseph Campbell
text: Follow your bliss: doors open where there were none.
q: What did Campbell advise?
action: Spend time on what lights you up.

author: Joseph Campbell
book: The Hero with a Thousand Faces
text: The cave you fear to enter holds the treasure you seek.
q: What holds the treasure?
action: Enter one 'cave' you've avoided.

author: C.S. Lewis
text: Humility is not thinking less of yourself but thinking of yourself less.
q: What is humility, per Lewis?
action: Focus on others in a conversation.

author: C.S. Lewis
text: Friendship is born when one person says to another: 'What! You too?'
q: When is friendship born?
action: Share an interest with someone.

author: J.R.R. Tolkien
text: All we have to decide is what to do with the time given to us.

a: What to do with our time.
action: Decide how to use one free hour.

author: J.R.R. Tolkien

action: Explore without a fixed goal.

author: John Gottman
book: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
text: Couples who thrive turn toward each other's small bids for attention.

action: Respond warmly to every bid from your partner today.

author: John Gottman
book: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
text: Criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling predict breakups.
q: What are the Four Horsemen?
action: Replace criticism with a gentle request.

author: John Gottman
book: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work

q: What is the magic ratio?
action: Add five positive moments today.

author: John Gottman
book: The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work
text: Build love maps: know your partner's world, worries and hopes.
q: What is a love map?
a: Knowledge of your partner's inner world.
action: Ask your partner about their current worries.

author: Gary Chapman
text: People feel loved through words, time, gifts, service or touch.
q: Name the five love languages.
a: Words of affirmation, quality time, gifts, acts of service, touch.
action: Show love in your partner's language.

author: Cicero
text: Friendship makes prosperity brighter and adversity lighter by sharing it.

action: Share good news with a friend.

author: Cicero
text: Friendship can only exist between good people.
q: Between whom can true friendship exist?
action: Be the friend you want.

author: Cicero
text: What is morally wrong can never be truly useful.
q: What can never be useful, per Cicero?
action: Reject a shortcut that's wrong.

author: Cicero
text: A room without books is like a body without a soul.
q: What is a room without books like?
action: Put a book where you'll see it.

author: Cicero
text: Old men keep their minds if they keep their interest and industry.
q: How do the old keep their minds?
action: Keep learning something new.

author: Proverbs
text: A soft answer turns away wrath.
q: What turns away wrath?
action: Answer harshness softly.

author: Proverbs
text: Go to the ant, sluggard; consider her ways and be wise — work in summer, store for winter.
q: What does the ant teach?
action: Prepare now for a slow season.

author: Proverbs

q: What goes before destruction?
action: Check your pride in a dispute.

author: Proverbs

action: Spend time with someone who challenges you.

action: Ask two people for advice.

action: Choose peace over winning.

author: Ecclesiastes

author: Ecclesiastes
text: Two are better than one; if one falls, the other lifts him up.

action: Help a friend up.

author: Ecclesiastes
text: Vanity of vanities — much striving is chasing the wind. Enjoy simple gifts.
q: What is much striving called?
action: Enjoy food and work simply today.

author: Job
text: Job lost everything yet kept integrity; suffering is not always punishment.
q: What does Job show?
action: Hold to integrity in a trial.

author: Psalms
text: Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.

action: Count how many weekends remain this year.

author: Matthew
text: Do not worry about tomorrow; tomorrow will worry about itself.

action: Focus only on today's tasks.

author: Matthew

action: Strengthen one foundation in life.

author: Luke
text: To whom much is given, much is required.

action: Use a gift to help others.

author: Corinthians
text: Love is patient and kind; it keeps no record of wrongs.

action: Forget one old wrong.

author: Talmud

action: Learn from someone unexpected.

author: Talmud
text: Who is rich? One who rejoices in his portion.

action: Rejoice in what you have.

author: Talmud
text: Who is strong? One who conquers his impulses.

action: Master one impulse.

author: Talmud
text: If I am not for myself, who will be? If I am only for myself, what am I? If not now, when?
q: What are Hillel's three questions?
action: Act on something now.

author: Talmud
text: Say little and do much.

action: Speak less, act more today.

author: Maimonides
text: Give a man a fish and you feed him for a day; teach him and you feed him for life (traditional saying).

action: Teach a skill instead of doing it for someone.

author: Ibn Khaldun
text: Group solidarity (asabiyyah) builds dynasties; luxury erodes it.

action: Strengthen team bonds over comfort.

author: Omar Khayyam
text: The moving finger writes and moves on; nothing can cancel a line.
q: What does the moving finger teach?
action: Let go of a past mistake.

author: Hafez
text: Even after all this time, the sun never says to the earth 'You owe me.'
q: What does the sun never say?
action: Give without keeping score.

author: Saadi
text: Human beings are members of a whole; when one suffers, all feel it.

a: We are members of a whole.
action: Help someone suffering.

author: Sun Tzu
text: Opportunities multiply as they are seized.

action: Seize one small opportunity.

author: Sun Tzu

a: One who knows when to fight.
action: Skip a fight not worth it.

author: Epicurus
text: Death is nothing to us: when we are, death is not; when death is, we are not.

author: Epicurus
text: It's impossible to live pleasantly without living wisely, honourably and justly.
q: What is necessary for a pleasant life?
action: Act justly today.

action: Tell a friend you're there for them.

author: Lucretius

action: Study a natural process.

author: Boethius
text: True happiness is not in fortune's gifts but in the highest good within.
q: Where is true happiness?
action: Find joy independent of possessions.

author: Boethius
text: Adversity reveals true friends; prosperity hides them.
q: What does adversity reveal?
action: Thank a friend who stood by you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Don't be ashamed to need help. Like a soldier storming a wall, you may need a hand.
q: What should we not be ashamed of?
action: Ask for help with one task.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Think of yourself as dead; now take what's left and live it properly.
q: What exercise does Marcus suggest?
action: Live the rest of today 'properly'.

author: Marcus Aurelius

q: What makes our life, per Marcus?
action: Notice your thoughts' effect on your mood.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be like the rocky headland on which waves constantly break; it stands firm.
q: What image does Marcus use for steadiness?
action: Stand firm under pressure.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From my grandfather: good morals and control of temper. Gratitude for our teachers.
q: How did Marcus begin Meditations?
a: Listing what he learned from others.
action: List what you learned from three people.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is ridiculous not to escape your own faults, which is possible, but to try to escape others', which isn't.
q: What is ridiculous, per Marcus?
a: Fleeing others' faults rather than our own.
action: Work on one of your own faults.

author: Seneca
text: The whole future lies in uncertainty: live immediately.
q: Why live immediately?
action: Do something meaningful now.

author: Seneca
text: Wherever there's a human being, there's an opportunity for kindness.
q: Where is there an opportunity for kindness?
action: Be kind to every person you meet.

author: Seneca
text: True happiness is to enjoy the present without anxious dependence on the future.
q: What is true happiness?
action: Enjoy one moment fully.

author: Seneca
text: Ask yourself daily: what weakness have I overcome today? What vice resisted?

a: What weakness overcome, what vice resisted.
action: Ask these tonight.

author: Seneca
text: Withdraw into yourself as much as you can; associate with those who make you better.
q: Who should we associate with?
action: Plan time with an uplifting person.

author: Seneca

q: Who is least able to live?
action: Cancel one unnecessary commitment.

author: Epictetus

q: Who is invincible?
action: Stay calm about something outside your control.

author: Epictetus
text: Be careful whom you associate with; it is human to imitate.
q: Why choose company carefully?
action: Notice whom you imitate.

author: Seneca
text: Set aside days to live on the scantiest food, and ask: 'Is this what I feared?'
q: What question follows voluntary poverty?
action: Skip one comfort and notice you're fine.

author: Seneca
text: Nothing is ours except time. Nature entrusted us with this fleeting thing.

author: Seneca
text: Our ancestors' discoveries were not final; much remains for future generations.
q: What did Seneca say of knowledge?
action: Learn something new about the world.

author: Seneca

action: Take the harder right path today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Look back over the past with its changing empires; you can foresee the future too.

action: Read history for 15 minutes.

author: Marcus Aurelius

q: What should we think of upon waking?
action: Say thanks on waking.

author: Marcus Aurelius

action: Step around an annoyance without complaint.

author: Marcus Aurelius

author: Marcus Aurelius

action: Reflect on living well to the end.

author: Epictetus

action: Study for 20 minutes.

author: Epictetus

author: Epictetus
text: Seek not that things happen as you wish but wish them as they happen.

action: Embrace an unplanned event.

author: Epictetus

author: Hierocles

author: Solon

action: Stop eating before you're full.

author: Benjamin Franklin

action: Avoid gossip today.

author: Benjamin Franklin
text: Order: let all your things have their places; let each part of business have its time.

author: Benjamin Franklin

author: Benjamin Franklin

q: How does Covey plan weekly?
action: Set one goal per role this week.

author: Stephen Covey
book: The 7 Habits of Highly Effective People

action: Do a loving act regardless of feeling.

author: Dale Carnegie

action: Write one thing you look forward to.

action: Visualise a meaningful future moment.

author: Viktor Frankl

action: Focus on someone else when anxious.
